      "value": "Side A's command: Marshal Davout led the 3rd corps in person. In the 3rd corps's journal he sent his first aide-de-camp, Colonel Burke, forward with a detachment of chasseurs to bring on a skirmish and get certain information on the enemy's position; General Gauthier had orders to receive the charge of the Prussian squadrons with a regiment of his brigade in square, and Davout, seeing his right outflanked, sent General Petit to that regiment's help with another, followed in echelon by a third, and brought guns forward; he, General Gudin and Generals Gauthier and Petit moved from one square to another, and not a battalion was broken although General Blücher returned to the charge again and again. When Friant's division came up he had a battery that hampered its movements carried by a battalion under Colonel Higonet and told Friant not to let himself be outflanked; he sent help to a regiment left alone on the left of Hassenhausen, and when Gudin's division, turned on its left, was about to give way, Morand's division arrived at the run and Davout went with Morand to its head; seeing the King's last effort to break in the French left, he sent Morand against it, and, profiting from the success of both wings, had the centre advance. From the start he had put all his cavalry on his right wing, the only part of his line where it could act effectively (all OCR so far). In Höpfner, as soon as Davout saw Prussian cavalry threatening his right he ordered the brigade Petit, on its arrival, to reinforce the regiment to the right of Hassenhausen, with another regiment and guns to the left of the village and skirmishers in it linking the two; he led Friant's battalions as they arrived against the right of Gudin's division, detached others of them at once to manoeuvre in the Prussian left flank and rear, and brought Morand's battalions up at a full run to reinforce and extend his left; and, fearing to be turned on his left from the Guards' position above Sulza, he sent a battalion along the Saale and the Ilm when Morand arrived and, when the Prussian divisions began to retreat, ordered Morand with a regiment and the division's artillery on Sonnendorf and the Sonnenberg. Höpfner's reflections say that the Prussians' visible inability to take Hassenhausen let Davout act early, under its cover, against their left wing, in whose prolongation lay their line of retreat, and that Morand's arrival let him use most of Friant's division and reach out as far as Lisdorf, having evidently nothing more to fear for his front (all OCR). At the end, by the journal, he directed a division onto the plateaus before Eckartsberga (OCR) and ordered General Petit to attack the last Prussian position with 400 men, and he bivouacked on the field (OCR). Davout's report praises Generals Friant, Gudin and Morand and General Daultanne, and the 5th Bulletin says he showed distinguished bravery and firmness of character and was seconded by Gudin, Friant, Morand and Daultanne, his chief of staff.",

      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Side B's command: the Duke of Brunswick commanded the main army, with the King present. On the evening before the battle the Duke, very weak and exhausted, thought not remotely of a battle between Auerstädt and Kösen and still believed he had to deal only with a detached corps of about 6000 French at Naumburg; the next day's movement was arranged with Field Marshal Möllendorf, Generals Kalkreuth, Schmettau, Wartensleben, Zastrow and Phull and Colonels Scharnhorst and Kleist present, no one from the division Oranien being there and General Blücher not yet arrived. In the morning the march set off in the fog; Möllendorf had Schmettau's main body follow its advanced guard immediately, and Höpfner thinks the eagerness to get at the enemy and catch the French cavalry beyond the defile was the main reason that the usual caution was dropped, the enemy and the ground left unreconnoitred and the lifting of the fog not awaited, Möllendorf vying with the youngest and the impulse reaching even the Duke. General Blücher, who found the King at the head of Schmettau's division and asked for instructions, was referred to the Duke and told only that some enemy cavalry regiments were said to have crossed the pass of Kösen and must be thrown back; on meeting French infantry he sent to the Duke asking for more cavalry and more troops to strike a decisive blow. After the first clash the Duke thought it doubtful to march on before the fog lifted, but Möllendorf believed they must march on without loss of time and the King, assuming they had not met considerable forces, agreed. The enemy was thought too strong to attack at once with the division Schmettau alone, so the division Wartensleben was first to come level, and the Duke made Colonel Scharnhorst responsible for everything on the left wing; the Duke sent the division Wartensleben to the right to take the height right of Hassenhausen, believing that if his infantry gained a footing there victory was certain, Möllendorf ordered the regiment Prinz Louis to take the village with the bayonet, and the Duke had called on a grenadier battalion to take the village when he was shot through both eyes; Schmettau was mortally wounded. Then all general arrangements ceased: the King took over the command definitively, but Möllendorf and every leader, aide-de-camp and staff officer gave orders as well, which was especially ruinous to the cavalry, led forward squadron by squadron. The King, displeased that the division Oranien had not come up sooner, ordered its battalions to reinforce the left wing of the fighting troops and then both wings, as the division Wartensleben could not hold much longer right of Hassenhausen. The reserve, first meant to march by Eckartsberga on Laucha, was ordered to follow the division Oranien through Auerstädt; when Captain Tiedemann of the general staff proposed once more to General Arnim, in Kalkreuth's absence, to march by Reisdorf to Eckartsberga and decide the battle by turning the enemy's right, the general would not depart from the order he had received, and Kalkreuth took no notice of Major Jagow's proposal to move part of the reserve on Lisdorf. The King, from the height of Eckartsberga, having given up hope of throwing the enemy back on Kösen, ordered the retreat, first toward Sömmerda and then on Weimar, to unite with Prince Hohenlohe and renew the battle the next day; he countermanded General Blücher's attack with the cavalry and had General Kalkreuth lead the army back (OCR from 'In the morning'). Höpfner's reflections say that on the Prussian side the passage from the march disposition to a plan of battle was wholly lacking: no one knew what to do and the troops went into the fight without knowing what was wanted; with an orderly plan the reserve would not have been split up nor 8 battalions spent covering the right flank, and the reserves would have marched by Eckartsberga to turn Davout's right. They also call it unwise to have let General Blücher attack the infantry his cavalry met in the fog, and say that after the Duke's mortal wound all unity in the arrangements for continuing the battle was lost, every general, staff officer and adjutant commanding on his own, and that the battle was given up before the reserves had been used (OCR from 'They also').",

      "rationale": "Höpfner's page images (pp. 364 and 485) and his narrative and reflections from the OCR. The decisions on the field — the march in the fog, the commitment of the divisions one by one, the King's assumption of command, the handling of the reserve and the order to retreat — were the Prussian commanders' own, so the claim is tagged commander_created. Höpfner's reflections also blame the organisation of the army command, which set beside the Duke a council headed by the King himself instead of leaving him the whole responsibility (OCR). The Duke's mortal wound is also in Davout's report and the 5th Bulletin (claim side-b-losses-reported). English renderings (ours): 'at this arrangement Field Marshal Möllendorf, Generals Kalkreuth, Schmettau, Wartensleben, Zastrow and Phull, Colonels Scharnhorst and Kleist and the Duke's aides-de-camp were present'; 'of the division Oranien nobody was present; General Blücher, who had been ordered to headquarters, was also still missing'; 'the Duke thought not remotely of a battle between Auerstädt and Kösen, but spoke at great length about the position to be taken beyond the Unstrut, and still believed he had to deal with a detached corps of only about 6000 French at Naumburg'; 'the Duke was extremely weak; the hardships of the preceding days, the mental exertions and anxieties about the situation of the army, had exhausted his strength' (p. 364); 'the eagerness to get at the enemy, and the hope of capturing or destroying the enemy cavalry that had gone over the defile, was probably the main reason that the caution otherwise observed was lost from view, the reconnaissance of the enemy and of the ground left undone and the lifting of the fog not awaited, but rather everyone pressed forward, in which the old Field Marshal Möllendorf vied with the youngest, and this impulse communicated itself even to the otherwise so deliberate Duke'; 'the advanced guard of the division Schmettau set off, and since, by the general view of things, it was thought that no interval from the advanced guard was needed, Field Marshal Möllendorf, arriving, ordered that General Count Schmettau should follow immediately with the main body of the division'; 'for his own person the general [Blücher] went forward and found the King at the head of the division Schmettau with the regiment Alvensleben'; 'on asking for instructions he was referred to the Duke, and received only the information that some enemy cavalry regiments were said to have crossed the pass of Kösen already, which had to be thrown back'; 'Colonel Scharnhorst, who had made the same discovery [an enemy infantry line close at hand], met the general [Blücher] there, who at once sent his adjutant, Rittmeister Count Goltz, back to the Duke to report to him that he — the general — was outflanking the enemy, and to ask for more cavalry and more troops in general, with which he then meant to strike a decisive blow'; 'the Duke had, as mentioned, thought it doubtful to continue the march before the fog had lifted. The King did indeed take over the command definitively, but Field Marshal Möllendorf, every single leader, every aide-de-camp, general staff officer etc.'; '[each] likewise made arrangements, which had an especially ruinous effect on the use of the cavalry, which was led forward and used squadron by squadron by everyone who wished to help here or there, so that all common direction of this arm ceased and, despite its superiority, it could nowhere gain a significant effect'; 'immediately afterwards the King had come, had expressed himself very displeased that the division [Oranien] had not come up sooner, and had ordered the left wing of the fighting troops to be reinforced with all battalions;'; 'while one was still busy deploying, a second order of the King had come: to reinforce both wings of the fighting troops, since the division Wartensleben would not be able to hold much longer to the right of Hassenhausen'; 'the two reserve divisions of General Count Kalkreuth were, according to the first arrangement, to march on Laucha'; 'a peasant from Auerstädt had offered to lead them by Reisdorf, Mallendorf, Eckartsberga and Lisdorf into the old road to Laucha, but the general had first had this way reconnoitred by a column guide, to whom it had not seemed wide enough, and when the fire began at Hassenhausen while the reserves still stood behind Auerstädt, it was thought necessary to bring them up for immediate support, and it was ordered that they should follow the division Oranien and, together with the ... battalion of Blücher hussars and part of the Württemberg hussars, halt as general reserve with Gernstädt before them'; 'when it was further noticed that, with the disorder in Auerstädt, a considerable time would also pass before the infantry of the reserve could pass the village, Captain Tiedemann of the general staff proposed to the division com-';       "id": "davout-decision",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Marshal Davout's decision: on the 13th, at the time a Prussian patrol threw back a French chasseur patrol, Davout was on the road from Kösen to Hassenhausen with his suite to reconnoitre the ground, and from the height behind Hassenhausen he saw the march of the advanced guard of the division Schmettau and part of the division itself; on his return to Naumburg he had the pass of Kösen occupied by the 25th line infantry regiment and assembled his generals. Napoleon's orders, dated 10 in the evening of the 13th from the heights by Jena, reached him only toward 3 in the morning of the 14th: Napoleon, resolved to attack the Prussian army between Jena and Weimar, called on him to direct himself on Apolda to act in its rear, leaving him the road; in the 5th Bulletin Davout had been ordered to debouch by Naumburg, to defend the defiles of Kösen if the enemy marched on Naumburg or to go to Apolda and take the enemy in the rear if he stayed in his position. Davout proposed that Marshal Bernadotte debouch behind him as far as Kösen and take command of the united corps of about 56,000 men, but Bernadotte understood the order otherwise and believed he must march to Dornburg. Davout had kept his generals at his quarters that night, and when the orders came they left at once to set their troops in motion (OCR). By the 3rd corps's journal there was no other road toward Erfurt by Auerstädt and Apolda, as the Emperor had ordered, so it was important to seize the head of the defile in order to deploy; by the marshal's orders given in the night, because of the distance of the 1st division, the movement was made by the left, and General Gudin with the 3rd division crossed the Saale on the bridge of Kösen at half past 6, Gudin's report having the division leave its position at Neuflemming at 4 in the morning and its head cross the defile at 6. Davout reported that, debouching from Kösen, he found the enemy a quarter of a league away, marching to seize that debouch himself, and that the battle was engaged at once. Höpfner says that at Kösen, as at Jena, everything depended on reaching a point on the plateau of the left bank before the Prussians (OCR).",

That he met the Prussian main army at Hassenhausen was not his choice (claim posture). Foucart's note to the journal's 'orders given in the night' refers to p. 670, where the 3rd corps set off immediately and the 3rd division was crossing the bridge at half past 6; the orders themselves are not in the passages read.       "id": "side-a-losses-reported",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side A's losses as reported: in the 3rd corps's journal the 1st division lost 98 officers and 2,181 men killed or wounded, the 2nd 20 and 900 and the 3rd 134 and 3,500, 252 officers and 6,581 men in all, and with the losses of the cavalry, artillery, engineers and staff about a third of the 3rd corps was put out of action. Davout reported that the Emperor had lost many brave men, among them General Debilly and Colonels Vergès, Higonet, Viala and Nicolas, with several others wounded, that several regiments had lost most of their officers, and that the number of wounded was very considerable. The 5th Bulletin, whose account covers Jena and Auerstedt together, estimates the French loss at 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded, regrets among the generals only General Debilly, and names among the colonels killed Vergès of the 12th line infantry regiment, Nicolas of the 61st, Viala of the 85th and Higonet of the 108th. Höpfner writes that the enemy himself gave his loss as 270 officers and 7000 men.",
      "status": "supported",

      "rationale": "Read from the page images (pp. 683, 684, 672, 673, 614, 619, 620 and 471). Bodart's 7,100 with 252 officers (claim bodart-losses) lies between the journal's three divisions and Höpfner's figure. The Bulletin's 1,000 or 1,100 killed and 3,000 wounded, 4,000 or 4,100 for both fields (our arithmetic), are fewer than the journal's 6,833 for the 3rd corps's infantry divisions alone. The Bulletin's dead colonels are not divided by field in the passages read; Vergès, Nicolas, Viala and Higonet are the four Davout names. Foucart's note to the journal's cavalry losses, a table of the losses of the 3rd corps's three chasseur regiments (p. 684, note 1), and the ordonnateur Chambon's letter to Davout on the wounded at Naumburg (p. 684, note 3) were read only in the OCR and are not restated, and the fuller details Davout's report promised were not looked for (open questions).       "value": "Side B's losses as reported: in the 3rd corps's journal the enemy lost 115 pieces of cannon, about 15,000 men killed or wounded and 3,000 prisoners, and at the end abandoned 20 pieces of cannon to General Petit. Davout reported that the victory remained with his corps together with almost all the enemy artillery, that the number of prisoners was not very considerable because his little cavalry could not exploit the infantry's successes, that the Duke of Brunswick was gravely wounded in the head and the wound thought mortal, that Prussian generals were wounded, among them Prince August, the King's uncle, and that the Guards on horse and on foot suffered much. The 5th Bulletin's results for Jena and Auerstedt together are 30,000 to 40,000 prisoners, among them more than 20 generals including Lieutenant-General Schmettau, 25 to 30 colours, 300 pieces of cannon and more than 20,000 killed or wounded, with Field Marshal Möllendorf wounded and the Duke of Brunswick killed. Höpfner holds a statement of the Prussian loss at Auerstädt impossible because of the uninterrupted retreat until the army's complete dissolution, and says the men's loss may be inferred from the officers': 1 field marshal, 3 generals, 7 staff officers and 36 other officers, 47 officers in all, were killed or died of wounds — the Duke of Brunswick, Lieutenant-General Count Schmettau and Major-Generals Quitzow and Greiffenberg — and 1 field marshal, 5 generals, 34 staff officers and 181 other officers, 221 in all without the general staff and adjutants, were wounded; 57 guns were lost without the battalion guns, and nearly half the infantry that stood against Hassenhausen was killed or wounded. His narrative calls the loss in prisoners great in the retreat of the left wing by Poppel and very considerable in the retreat by Reisdorf, and his reflections call it very considerable among the Prussians beaten in front; for single units he gives losses for the Irwing dragoons and the fusilier battalion Greiffenberg (OCR from 'His narrative', figures not restated).",

      "id": "auerstedt-ground",
      "dimension": "terrain",
      "value": "Auerstädt is a village in the Prussian province of Saxony, 22 km north of Jena (Bodart). In the 3rd corps's journal the ground beyond the Saale is high and offers fine plateaus, cut here and there by brooks, small ravines and some sunken roads and dotted with many villages, crowned to the north by higher knolls covered with clumps of wood; the Saale is not fordable and its left bank is very steep; the great road from Naumburg to Weimar and Erfurt passes through Kösen, where there is a stone bridge over the Saale, and beyond it one must climb a long, steep slope to the plateau of Hassenhausen. Höpfner calls the defile of Kösen an unassailable post, scarcely 1½ Meilen from the division Schmettau's camp before Auerstädt, and says that, with the road as it then was, the slightest infantry or artillery detachment could have made the climb from the Saale to the plateau impossible (the last OCR). A fog so thick that objects could not be made out at pistol range rose half an hour before daybreak (the journal) and cleared gradually (Höpfner; both OCR). Hassenhausen formed the pivot of Davout's position, with no new hold for his corps until behind the Saale if it were lost, and Höpfner judges that taking it would have decided the battle, since the French had very little cavalry and without the village could no longer hold the plain between it and the Saale; the French in it stood covered up to the neck in the hollow roads, in the houses and behind the hedges, and the Prussians came early into the French fire, which the village's gardens covered (OCR). Battalions of the division Friant, detached by Davout on their arrival, manoeuvred in the Prussian left flank and rear on ground where they had nothing to fear from the superior Prussian cavalry (Höpfner), and Davout put his cavalry on his right, the only part of his line where it could act; the Prussian outflanking movement came first against that wing, where the plain was more open and the folds of ground on the way from Poppel toward Spielberg let the columns climb under cover (Foucart's notes; all OCR).",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "inherited",
      "rationale": "Bodart's place note, read from the page image in the frame transcription; the journal (p. 673) and Höpfner (p. 364) from the page images; the rest from the OCR. The ground and the fog were there before the battle, so the claim is inherited; Davout's push to seize the head of the defile and deploy on the plateau is claim davout-decision. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(village in Prussia, province of Saxony, 22 km north of Jena)'; the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); 'the ground beyond the Saale is high and offers fine plateaus, which are cut here and there by some brooks, by small ravines and some sunken roads, and over which a great number of villages are spread'; 'these plateaus are crowned toward the north by higher knolls covered with clumps of wood'; 'the Saale is not fordable; its left bank is very steep and also covered with some clumps of wood'; 'the great road from Naumburg to Weimar and Erfurt passes through Kösen, where there is a stone bridge over the Saale'; 'after crossing this river one must climb by a steep and long slope onto the plateau of Hassenhausen' (p. 673); Höpfner, 'the division Schmettau had from its camp before Auerstädt to the defile of Kösen scarcely 1½ Meilen, and could therefore very well still reach this unassailable post on the 13th, as the disposition had indeed prescribed, and scarcely could a forced march have been more justified anywhere;' (p. 364); 'at Kösen this was all the more necessary since, with the direction and condition at that time of the road from the Saale to the plateau, the slightest infantry and artillery detachment could have made the climb of the left edge of the valley impossible' (OCR); the journal, 'half an hour before day a fog had risen so thick that it did not allow objects to be made out at pistol range' (OCR); Höpfner, 'the fog had gradually cleared'; 'Hassenhausen thus formed the pivot of the marshal's position, to which the detachments arriving little by little could attach themselves.       "value": "Side A: all the 3rd corps's artillery, reserve included, consisted of only 44 pieces of different calibres (the journal); Davout had little cavalry, not enough to profit from the infantry's successes, the grand-duc de Berg having withdrawn the dragoon division Sahuc the day before; and by Davout's later complaint his cavalry general, Viallanes, despite his entreaties left the marshal's quarters, where the generals were to spend the night, without his knowledge and could not be found when the orders came, so that his cavalry, instead of debouching first, debouched three hours later (OCR). About 7 in the evening, with cartridges lacking and the units much weakened, Davout took position, and the cartridges were to be replaced in the night. Side B: the Prussian divisions reached their bivouacs late, in the cold, dark night, and wood, straw and food could not be brought in under proper supervision, which ended in the plundering of the villages nearby; the troops had cooked and drawn bread, the filled bread wagons were left behind on the Duke's order, and the King's gift of brandy reached few of the troops (OCR). Höpfner's reflections on Auerstädt say the troops went into battle the next morning exhausted and dispirited, without straw, wood and food, and his reflections on both battles that in the rich country the army could not bring itself to requisition and let men and horses go hungry (OCR). On the field the battalion guns of the division Wartensleben stuck in part in the hollow it crossed between Rehhausen and Tauchwitz; guns of the battery Riemer, assigned to the grenadier battalion Rheinbaben, which the King personally ordered forward against Poppel as the division Oranien came up, overturned in the road ditch, and those that could follow had only a few rounds with them, the ammunition wagons not having come up; and with several Prussian battalions the ammunition was already shot off when Morand's division attacked (OCR).",

No return of ammunition or supply on hand for either side was found in the passages read.       "id": "side-b-information",
      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Side B's information: on the day before the battle a Prussian patrol under Lieutenant Böhmer met a French patrol between Auerstädt and Kösen, threw it back and took a chasseur, who stated that General Davout had taken Naumburg the day before with his division; it seemed certain that chasseur regiments had crossed the defile of Kösen, and reports put infantry with guns at the pass and bridge of Kösen and more infantry at Naumburg, all of Davout's corps, but on the whole the news of the enemy was contradictory, and the troops arrived too late for any proper reconnaissance of the ground and the enemy; in the night no further news of the enemy and no significant outpost reports reached headquarters at Auerstädt, so everything ordered for crossing the Unstrut at Freiburg and Laucha stayed in force (all OCR so far). The Duke still believed he faced a detached corps of only about 6000 French at Naumburg, and the statements of the head forester at Auerstädt did not change his view. In the morning the Duke remarked to Colonel Scharnhorst that it was a very doubtful thing to advance so, not knowing what was before them (OCR); when the Prussians met the enemy in the fog they believed it only a detachment, and Höpfner holds that once it was certain that a considerable enemy corps was arriving the march dispositions should have been dropped. Later the Prussians judged the enemy far stronger than he was, because they had themselves lost heavily and he had husbanded his forces, and saw the divisions of their main body destroyed while the enemy still showed fresh forces and perhaps further reinforcement from Kösen (OCR). By the account of an officer taken prisoner and brought to the King, which Colonel Blein heard, the King, told that Davout's corps was only 25,000 to 26,000 men, called it French bragging and said there were certainly more than 50,000; and he did not yet know that Hohenlohe and Rüchel had been completely defeated at Jena the same day when he appointed Weimar as the general rendezvous.",

      "value": "Side B's objectives: by Höpfner's reflections the Duke did not wish to fight but to march off to the left, cross the Unstrut and place himself again directly before the French, the main army marching off while Prince Hohenlohe was to cover the right flank of its march and then follow (OCR). The disposition for the main army's march announced a retrograde movement, to unite with Duke Eugen of Württemberg and to free the army's rear again, for which the division Schmettau was to set off at once and march to Kösen, taking the pass if it was not strongly held (OCR); Höpfner holds that the division could well have reached that unassailable post on the 13th, as the disposition had prescribed, but the march to Auerstädt was thought long enough and the Duke did not think it urgent. His reflections say the course of the battle had been prepared by the arrangements of the 13th, among them that the division was not sent forward to Kösen that afternoon to occupy the pass and so make sure that the next day's march on Freyburg would not be disturbed: with the pass held, he says, the battle of Auerstädt became impossible (OCR from 'among them'). When a prisoner's report on Davout came in, the Duke had the troops of the main army hasten their march and be ready to engage the enemy that same day, the King intending to attack him at once (OCR). For the next day, as arranged late in the evening at Auerstädt, the army was to set off at daybreak in the same order of march, the division Schmettau following the road to Kösen, its cavalry and advanced guard throwing themselves on the enemy cavalry and an infantry brigade taking and occupying the post of Kösen, the division holding the heights of Kösen until the whole army had passed behind it and defiled across the Unstrut, while the two reserve divisions marched by Eckartsberga straight on Laucha (OCR). In Goltz's account the main army meant to cross the Unstrut between Freyburg and Laucha on the 14th to join the reserve corps approaching the Saale. Höpfner's reflections add that the battle was fought not only to win a victory but to open the retreat across the Unstrut toward the Saale and the middle Elbe, which obliged the Prussians to dare the utmost (OCR). After the battle the King, still hoping to join Prince Hohenlohe and General Rüchel, appointed Weimar as the general rendezvous.",

      "value": "Both sides attacked. Davout reported that, debouching from Kösen, he found the enemy a quarter of a league off, marching to seize that debouch himself, and that the battle was engaged at once. Höpfner calls it, on both sides, a matter of dispositions after a chance encounter ('Rencontre'), both being surprised by running into a considerable opponent; the heads of both armies met at Hassenhausen, which the French occupied, and the division Gudin and the Prussian division Schmettau reached it at about the same time (the last OCR). The Prussians attacked: General Blücher's cavalry attacked the French infantry at Hassenhausen and was repulsed by the squares; the King ordered the division Schmettau to attack, and Schmettau's and Wartensleben's divisions attacked Hassenhausen but could not take it, the Duke having called on a grenadier battalion to take the village when he was shot; Prince Wilhelm's cavalry charged Morand's division, which received it in square (OCR). The French attacked: while Gudin's division held at Hassenhausen, Friant's went on turning the enemy, advancing between Spielberg and Zeckwar against the Prussian left; Davout sent Morand's division against the King's last effort to break the French left, and Morand outflanked the Prussian army and took it in flank; Davout then had the centre advance (OCR); at the end General Petit, ordered to attack the last Prussian position before Eckartsberga with 400 men, climbed the height with the bayonet without returning the fire and took 20 pieces of cannon.",

### B373b: KAPITULATION von Erfurt (15./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p373, as printed:

```text
1806 15./10. KAPITULATION von Erfurt
(Stadt in Preußen, Provinz Sachsen, 20 km westl. von Weimar).
Die Franzosen unter Großherzog Murat zwingen 10.000 Preußen unter Gen.-Lt. Pz. v. Oranien zur Übergabe. Die preußischen Truppen durften mit Kriegsehren ausziehen, mußten jedoch auf dem Glacis die Waffen niederlegen und sich kriegsgefangen geben. Den Offizieren (worunter 1 GFM., 6 Gen.) wurde gegen die ehrenwörtliche Verpflichtung, vor ihrer Auswechslung nicht gegen Frankreich zu dienen, freier Abzug bewilligt. Die Franzosen fanden in Erfurt 65 Geschütze vor.
```

      "value": "Höpfner: the Prince of Orange had arrived in Erfurt, and after him Field Marshal Möllendorf, who had the prince assemble the generals and staff officers on the Petersberg; towards noon Möllendorf gave the definite order for the baggage to leave at once for Langensalza and the cavalry and the infantry to follow at set hours. General Larisch at once left his position on the Galgenberg with the infantry and fell back in disorder to the town. Having received the King's order to march to Sömmerda, Larisch resolved to carry it out at once, but the prince had him halt and, on the Petersberg, repeated the order, since getting through was no longer possible; when Larisch appealed to the King's order, the prince gave the strict order that he stay in Erfurt with the troops and have the walls manned. The commandant, Major Prüschenk, at first meant to defend himself seriously but soon changed his mind; Möllendorf attended only the start of the negotiations. The prince dictated the points of the capitulation to Major Lossau of the general staff. Höpfner judges that not defending the town was in order, but that it would then have been a duty to take the troops out at once to continue the retreat under the Duke of Weimar's protection, and that the surrender of the Petersberg was irresponsible: against a regular attack it could have held out 19 days.",

      "id": "capitulation",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Erfurt on 15 October: the Prussian troops marched out with the honours of war, laid down their arms on the glacis and became prisoners of war; the officers, among them a field marshal and six generals, were released on their word not to serve against France until exchanged. Höpfner says the capitulation was concluded in the night to the 16th; men from the Bayreuth country were sent home and the rest treated as prisoners of war. The terms the major general sent Murat as the only capitulation His Majesty could grant were that the troops march out with the honours of war, file through the middle of the French army and lay down their arms, the soldiers keeping their booty and the officers their baggage; all were to be prisoners of war, the soldiers and even the generals to be sent to France, though the Emperor left Murat latitude to let the officers go home on their undertaking not to serve before their exchange.       "value": "Side B's loss: Bodart has the 10,000 Prussians surrender, lay down their arms on the glacis and become prisoners of war, their officers released on parole, and the French find 65 guns in Erfurt. }

### B374a: TREFFEN bei Halle (17./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p374, as printed:

```text
1806 17./10. TREFFEN bei Halle (4.)
(Stadt in Preußen, Provinz Sachsen, an der Saale, 32 km nordwestl. von Leipzig).
Sieg der Franzosen (14.500 Inft., 1.500 Kav. = 16.000 M.) unter Marschall Bernadotte über die Preußen (18 Btln., 20 Esk. = 11.500 Inft., 2.200 Kav., 62 Kan. = 13.700 M.) unter Gen. d. Kav. Hz. E. v. Württemberg.
Frz. Verl.: ca. 800 M. (6 Stb.-, 28 Ob.-Offz.) tot u. verw.
Preuß. Verl.: 1.000 M. tot u. verw. 4.200 „ Gefg. zus. 5.200 M. (113 Offz.) = 37% 11 Kan., 4 Fahnen.
[Offiziersverlust table not transcribed]
```

      "value": "Höpfner: the Duke, though informed of the beaten army's retreat, could not bring himself to leave Halle, believing he must first gather all his troops and holding the King's order to keep large stores ready at Halle for the army; so the retreat was not begun and even the baggage stayed with the corps.       "value": "Höpfner: the King's order reached the Duke on his journey to Halle; on the onward journey he heard the cannonades of Jena and Auerstedt and concluded, from the King's letter and the fire receding, that the enemy's turning movement had been beaten off; half a day then passed without his receiving news of the previous day's battles, and the reports that came in contradicted each other; then came a report of Davout at Naumburg and Weißenfels, and a wounded officer of the regiment Renouard told him of the main army's defeat. He was also informed of the beaten army's retreat by the Halberstadt chamber, and in Höpfner's view sufficiently informed of the army's state by General Tschammer. When the attack came, a hussar officer back from patrol had reported only an hour before that nothing of the enemy had been seen near Merseburg and Lauchstädt; the dragoons' outpost was attacked so unexpectedly that the regiment was rather surprised, and the Duke took the attack for a reconnaissance.",

### B374b: KAPITULATION von Spandau (25./10. 1806)

```text
1806 25./10. KAPITULATION von Spandau
(Befestigte Stadt in Preußen, Brandenburg, 9 km westl. von Berlin).
Die preußische Garnison (1.000 M.) unter Major v. Benekendorf ergibt sich ohne Schwertstreich an die Franzosen unter Marschall Lannes.

      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Major Benekendorf, the commandant, wrote to the King that the citadel was secure against a coup de main and that, failing other orders, he would leave the enemy only the ruins of the fortress. The commandant's reply to the summons made to him, a copy of which went with Lannes's letter, was that the fortress would not surrender but would not oppose the passage of the French troops entering by the Potsdam gate and leaving by the Charlottenburg gate, provided they did not approach the fortress, its bridges and its gates. In Höpfner's account the commandant called a council of war in which all the members but the engineer captain Meinert voted to surrender, though no shot had yet been fired, citing the bad state of the works, the insufficient ammunition and garrison and the harm a defence would do to the King's interest and the inhabitants'. He declared to the parlementaire his readiness to surrender, the judge-advocate was to draw up the points of capitulation, and during this work he is said to have waved his handkerchief to the post at the drawbridge to let it down. He was later sentenced to be shot, and pardoned by the King to fortress imprisonment for life. Bertrand reported that a young officer said only that they had the King's order to defend themselves and would die, and that the commandant is old.",

      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Spandau on 25 October: the garrison surrendered without a fight to the French under Lannes. ### B374c: KAPITULATION von Prenzlau (28./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p374, as printed:

```text
1806 28./10. KAPITULATION von Prenzlau
(Stadt in Preußen, Brandenburg, am Ausfluß der Ucker aus dem Uckersee, 120 km nordöstl. von Potsdam).
Die Franzosen unter Großherzog Murat nötigen die preußische Armee unter Gen. d. Inf. Fürst Hohenlohe zur Kapitulation, wonach 10.000 M. (wor. 400 Offz.) in Kriegsgefangenschaft gerieten, 45 Fahnen, 64 Geschütze, 1.800 Pferde den Franzosen in die Hände fielen.
```

    {
      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: General Tschammer was charged with the defence of the approaches to Prenzlau; his companies and battalion guns covered the Berliner-Damm while two companies held the Berliner-Thor. He told the first parlementaire that he would continue his march without firing first, but whispered to General Hirschfeld that they were surrounded, and let Colonel Massenbach ride back with the parlementaire to see the enemy for himself. An officer of his suite, whose name was not established, ordered the grenadier battalion Dohna and the Wobeser dragoons back behind the town; Major Dohna left the gate despite Colonel Böhmke's order, and what caused this retreat Höpfner could not establish. Massenbach reported that they were not yet turned but might be in a few moments, that the Stettin road was open to the enemy and the enemy in the town, and urged that only pride and ambition could sacrifice the 7—8000 men still under the Prince's command; he assured General Hirschfeld that they were enclosed. Hohenlohe paid little attention to Captain Schöler's report and rode to meet Belliard; Hirschfeld was against any capitulation, and when Rittmeister Marwitz proposed falling on the small body standing in front, the Prince answered that Marshal Soult stood there. He reserved the terms for his generals and staff officers and obtained a longer truce. Before them he declared them surrounded and the road to Stettin cut, as Massenbach had seen for himself; Colonel Hüser, his chief of artillery, reported a want of ammunition, the guns having on average only 5—8 rounds, though he had only the battalion guns in view; the Prince called it his duty to accept the terms, all were silent, and he ordered the terms announced to the troops.       "id": "capitulation",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Prenzlau on 28 October: the French under Murat forced the Prussian army under Hohenlohe to capitulate. Murat wrote the same day that Hohenlohe and his corps were in his power: the officers were prisoners of war, keeping their swords and baggage and free to go home until exchanged; the troops laid down their arms, were prisoners of war and were sent to France. Höpfner gives the terms the Prince announced: the officers to keep their swords, horses and equipages and the men their knapsacks; the officers released on their word of honour not to serve until exchanged; the Guards and the King's regiment to be quartered at Potsdam; the NCOs and men of all other troops to go to France until exchanged; the arms not to be laid down but only stacked. The arms were stacked and the cavalry dismounted while the French shouted 'Vive l'Empereur!'.",

English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Murat, as in claim side-b-strength for the heading and date; 'Sire, Your Majesty's orders are carried out. The Prince of Hohenlohe is in my power, as is his army corps'; 'the officers are prisoners of war, keep their swords and baggage and may return home until the exchange; the troops have laid down their arms, are prisoners of war and are sent back to France'; Höpfner, 'the officers keep their swords, horses and equipages, the common soldier his knapsack' (OCR); 'the officers are released on their word of honour not to serve until the exchange, and are free to go wherever they think fit' (OCR); 'to the royal Guards, as to His Majesty the King's regiment, although this is already captured, Potsdam shall be assigned as residence' (OCR); 'the NCOs and privates of all other troops shall be taken back to France until the exchange' (OCR); 'the muskets shall not be laid down but only stacked, the troops march off and leave them' (OCR); 'the thing was done!       "id": "side-b-losses",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side B's loss: Bodart has 10,000 men (among them 400 officers) taken prisoner and 45 flags, 64 guns and 1,800 horses fallen to the French. Höpfner puts the troops that fell to the enemy by the capitulation itself at probably not over 10,000 men and 1800 horses. In the fighting before it the King's regiment, 25 officers and 701 men, fell into the enemy's power in the suburb; the grenadier company Taubenheim, 3 officers and 138 men, was partly cut down, partly taken, and General Tschammer with it; the Prittwitz dragoons, 375 horses strong, lost 2 officers and 20 dragoons killed and 5 officers, 97 dragoons and 120 horses wounded and captured; Lieutenants Linstow II and Rothkirch II of those dragoons fell and 7 officers were wounded; and the horse battery Studnitz-Schorlemmer was lost but for 2 guns. Of the captured men surely half ran off from the first night quarters. ### B374d: KAPITULATION von Stettin (29./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p374, as printed:

```text
1806 29./10. KAPITULATION von Stettin
(Hafenstadt in Preußen, an der Oder, Hauptstadt von Pommern).
Vor 800 französischen Husaren unter Brig.-Gen. Gf. Lasalle kapituliert ohne Schwertstreich die von 5.300 Preußen (wor. 100 Offz.) mit 281 Kan. unter GM. v. Romberg besetzte Festung. Die Offiziere wurden auf Ehrenwort entlassen, die Mannschaft geriet in Kriegsgefangenschaft.
```

      "id": "side-a-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "The capitulation records that Lasalle summoned Fort Preussen and the town of Stettin in the name of the Grand Duke of Berg and repeated the summons with insistence after a first refusal. Höpfner: a hussar officer with a trumpeter rode at a trot to the governor, unescorted and without a blindfold, summoned him in the Grand Duke's name and urged that all resistance was vain, since the fortress was surrounded by 100,000 men and Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated at Prenzlau; at 4 in the afternoon a second parlementaire declared that Lasalle stood with the advance guard ½ mile from the town, that the corps of Murat and Lannes would take the fortress the next morning with 30 to 40,000 men, and that if the governor did not surrender within 12 hours the town would have to pay ½ million Thaler besides the contribution to be demanded of it. The parlementaire accepted the governor's draft except the free withdrawal, and in the night brought it back translated into French with that condition changed to the garrison's disadvantage. Belliard, sent by Murat to Stettin to summon the commandant, found that Lasalle had begun the work and let him finish it, having the replies to the governor's demands put in; he approved the capitulation by the Grand Duke's order. Lasalle came into the town with cavalry at 6 in the morning to sign it.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "The capitulation's preamble, Belliard's letter and his approval, and Höpfner's account, all read from the page images. The parlementaires' figures are their claims, not counts. The parlementaire accepted them, but with the exception of the condition of free withdrawal, so the draft was signed by the governor and both commandants and handed to the parlementaire, who went back with it to General Lasalle'; 'in the night to the 30th the parlementaire returned to Stettin and brought back the draft translated into French, with the condition altered to the garrison's disadvantage, by which it was granted the fate of Hohenlohe's corps'; 'General Lasalle had already come into the town with cavalry in the morning at 6 o'clock to sign the capitulation, so that enemy troops were thus already in the fortress before the capitulation was signed'; Belliard, 'General Belliard to the major général. 30 October 1806'; 'I had been sent by the Prince to Stettin to summon the commandant, but Lasalle had begun the job and I let him finish it, having the replies put to the governor's demands'; 'by order of His Highness the Grand Duke of Berg and Cleves, lieutenant of the Emperor, the present capitulation seen and approved, to be carried out.     {
      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: the governor was the 81-year-old General-Lieutenant Romberg and the commandant Major General Knobelsdorf, and General Rauch, director of the engineering academy and in charge of the works, was named vice-commandant by the King. The governor kept back no man of the troops passing through for fortress duty and refused General Bila II passage, which by Höpfner's account caused the capitulation of Anklam. Romberg answered the first summons with apparent calm that he knew his duty and would defend the fortress entrusted to him to the utmost, but as soon as the parlementaire had gone he dictated to the judge-advocate Dragaud a draft capitulation: the fortress to be handed over the next morning, the garrison to have free withdrawal and march off with all marks of honour; the commandant and vice-commandant joined in, the latter dictating the end of the draft. At the second parlementaire the governor lost all composure; everyone talked at once in the Frenchman's presence and no one thought of calling the prescribed council of war; the minister Ingersleben, who had come in uninvited, took the parlementaire to his residence so that they could deliberate, and those present unanimously resolved to surrender. The governor and both commandants signed the draft. When the garrison, knowing nothing of the negotiation, fired on enemy horsemen riding too boldly forward, the governor forbade the firing. Romberg was sentenced to death by court martial in 1809 but pardoned by the King. Belliard called him an old wreck of a governor who greeted the French with a few cannon shots and surrendered at discretion after making many difficulties.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Side B's conduct from Höpfner, read from the page images of pp. 216-219, and Belliard's letter from the page image of p. 527. Höpfner does not name his sources for Stettin. So the parlementaire was dispatched at 1 o'clock midday with a refusal'; 'unfortunately these heroic sentiments of the governor were of very short duration; for hardly had the parlementaire gone when he dictated to the government's judge-advocate Dragaud a draft capitulation whose substance was: that the fortress should be handed over the next morning, and the garrison receive free withdrawal and march off with all marks of honour'; 'while they were still in full work, the commandant and vice-commandant also appeared, and the latter was charged with dictating the end of the draft, which was readily done'; 'the governor had lost all composure; he did not know what to answer the parlementaire and told him to be patient'; 'during this conversation the two commandants and several other officers of the garrison had come in; everyone talked at once in the presence of the Frenchman, and no-'; '-body thought of calling the prescribed council of war'; 'at last the minister Ingersleben, who had come in uninvited, took the parlementaire to his residence so that they could deliberate. Those present unanimously resolved to surrender'; as in claim side-a-command for the signing; 'the garrison, which had no idea of the negotiation begun, meanwhile fired on the enemy horsemen riding forward too boldly. The governor forbade the firing'; 'General Romberg was sentenced to death by court martial in 1809, but pardoned by the King'; Belliard, as in claim side-a-command for the heading; 'the old wreck of a governor greeted us with a few cannon shots and ended by surrendering at discretion after making many difficulties'.",

      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Stettin on 29 October without a stroke of the sword: the officers were released on their word of honour and the men went into captivity. The capitulation, dated at Stettin on 29 October 1806 at 6 in the evening and signed by Romberg as governor, surrendered the town and Fort Preussen to Lasalle. To the garrison's request for free exit with arms and baggage it answered that the garrison would march out with the honours of war, lay down its arms on the glacis and be prisoners of war sent to France, the officers prisoners on parole with passports to go where they wished, keeping their swords, baggage, horses and all that belonged to them; everything in the place belonging to the King of Prussia was to be handed over, the Prussian troops had until noon to settle their affairs, and the Berlin gate and a post on the Oder bridge were to be occupied by the French at 6 in the morning. Below the date the print sets the words 'seen and approved the present capitulation to be carried out' above Romberg's name, followed by Lasalle's, as brigadier general, at the headquarters of Möhringen on 29 October; whose approval the words record is not shown. Belliard approved the capitulation by the Grand Duke's order at half past eleven that evening. Belliard wrote that the commandant capitulated at 1 in the morning. Höpfner: the capitulation was carried out; at daybreak General Knobelsdorf led the garrison out by the Berlin gate, held like the Uckermünde gate by French cavalry, and it laid down its arms before 800 enemy cavalry and 2 guns. Lasalle reported that after he left, the garrison left on the glacis tried to take up its arms again, 500 having done so, until the elite battalion made them surrender again without firing a shot.",

Articles 11 and 12, printed without replies, hand over the treasure in the place and name artillery and engineer officers to hand over and receive the magazines, munitions, maps and plans. Lannes wrote on 31 October that after the capitulation a rumour that the Russians were coming had made part of the garrison take up arms again, and that all was back in order (OCR). ### B375a: KAPITULATION von Pasewalk (29./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 29./10. KAPITULATION von Pasewalk
(Stadt in Preußen, Pommern, an der Ucker, 37 km westl. von Stettin).
Vor der französischen Kavalleriebrigade Milhaud (700 Reiter) kapitulieren 4.200 Preußen, (worunter 185 Offiziere) mit 2.100 Pferden, 8 Kanonen, 1 Munitionswagen unter Brigadier Oberst v. Hagen, wonach die Offiziere auf Ehrenwort entlassen, die Mannschaften in Kriegsgefangenschaft abgeführt wurden.
```

      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Colonel Hagen, as the eldest of the column, called all the staff officers of the infantry and cavalry to a conference. Before it, Colonel Poser told the cavalry's staff officers that Prince Hohenlohe had capitulated and the pass at Löcknitz was occupied, so that they would have to cut their way through; Major Thielan of the Heising regiment spoke first of the difficulties a break-through faced with men and horses exhausted and told Lieutenant Prittwitz, who declared a capitulation dishonourable, to be quiet; Colonel Winning of the Leib-Karabiniers consulted not only his officers but also called into counsel the sergeant-major of each squadron with NCOs and men, and that meeting resolved that they could not cut through but must capitulate. Several staff officers urged Poser to set out for Stettin as soon as possible. At the conference Hagen said he lacked the knowledge to judge whether the cavalry could march on; the Landrat Podewils proposed a safe route by Jägerbrück and Stolzenburg, and the colonel, by the context Hagen, paid no heed. Poser posted no field guards and ordered no patrols, only a chain of posts round the bivouac whose officers were to meet the enemy with a trumpeter and tell him negotiations were under way, and sent officer after officer to find the enemy, Count Matuschka with orders to tell him of their sad situation and bring back an officer of higher rank to capitulate, but by no means to reconnoitre. When Prince Gustav of Mecklenburg-Schwerin reported the cavalry ever more enclosed and saw no way out but capitulation, Hagen, physically and morally exhausted and deeply bowed by Prenzlau, was confirmed in a resolve to capitulate that Höpfner says Poser seems to have prompted. Hagen and Poser signed a written mandate to capitulate for the two brigades with free withdrawal or, failing that, to surrender them into captivity. Höpfner finds no justification of any kind for the capitulation: the commanders thought of nothing but capitulation and sent officers in all directions to seek out the enemy and offer themselves.",

Because of the difficulty of the crossing he advised against a march to the island of Usedom' (OCR); 'the colonel paid no heed to this statement' (OCR); 'Colonel Poser arranged that for the night no field guards were posted and no patrolling ordered, but only a chain of posts drawn round the bivouac of the cavalry, whose commanding officers received the instruction, if the enemy approached, to enter into no hostilities but to go to meet him with a trumpeter and inform him that negotiations were already under way' (OCR); 'at midnight Colonel Poser further sent off Lieutenant Count Königsdorf of the Henckel cuirassiers with a trumpeter and ... men' (OCR); 'when this officer came back without having perceived anything of the enemy, Colonel Poser sent Lieutenant Count Matuschka of the same regiment with the same escort, but with the errand to ride straight on until he came upon the enemy, to inform him of their sad situation, and to bring back an officer of higher rank to capitulate, but by no means to make a reconnaissance' (OCR); 'they were informed early of the events at Prenzlau, and so knew of the enemy's approach; nevertheless no patrols are sent out to learn the enemy's position; no attempt is made, by spending their last strength, to forestall the enemy at Löcknitz; nor, if they believed they could not risk this attempt, do they take the trouble to inquire whether other roads than that by Löcknitz to Stettin were free; they pay no heed to the statement of the Landrat Podewils, who shows such a road; ### B375b: KAPITULATION von Boldekow (30./10. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 30./10. KAPITULATION von Boldekow
(Dorf in Preußen, Pommern, 14 km südl. von Anklam).
Die Franzosen unter Marschall Lannes nötigen die Bedeckungsmannschaft des Blücher'schen Artillerieparks unter Major v. Höpfner zur Kapitulation, wonach 25 Kanonen, 48 Munitionswägen, 800 Pferde in die Hände des Feindes und ca. 600 M. in Kriegsgefangenschaft gerieten.
```

      "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Major Höpfner led the artillery column, which Blücher had urged to make particular haste. At Rheinsberg, when Prince Hohenlohe's expected orders failed to come and news arrived of a fight of Blücher's rear guard, he judged it unwise either to march on Fürstenberg or to spend the night at Rheinsberg, and marched by Alt-Strelitz towards Woldeck; at Bredenfelde, hearing that Pasewalk was in the enemy's hands, he turned to Friedland. There he told General Bila I that he meant to follow him to Anklam the next day, but Bila sent word that he should not march to Anklam but take his measures at his own discretion. In great perplexity the major called all the officers together to decide where to turn if they could march neither to Anklam nor to Stettin, and they resolved to march to Boldekow for forage. There, hearing that the enemy was pushing into Mecklenburg, they sent Lieutenant Braun II with a trumpeter towards Pasewalk to see how far the enemy had come; when the French officer came back with him, it was thought that a capitulation had to be made. Höpfner adds that no one thought of destroying the artillery material or of saving the men on the horses still found fit.",

It was not long, however, before General Bila sent back and had the major told that he should not march to Anklam, but take his measures at his discretion'; 'Major Höpfner was in great perplexity about what to do next, and assembled all the officers to deliberate where to turn if they could march neither to Anklam nor to Stettin'; 'it was therefore decided to march first, on the morning of the 30th, to the nearest Prussian village, Boldekow, so as at least to get forage'; 'in Boldekow came the news that the enemy was pushing into Mecklenburg, which was confirmed by a patrol coming from Friedland'; 'Lieutenant Braun II of the artillery was now sent with a trumpeter in the direction of Pasewalk to see how far the enemy had advanced'; as in claim side-a-strength for his meeting with the enemy and the French officer; as in claim side-b-strength for the capitulation; 'no one thought of destroying the artillery material or of trying to save the men on the horses still found fit'.",

### B375c: KAPITULATION von Küstrin (1./11. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 1./11. KAPITULATION von Küstrin
(Stadt in Preußen, Brandenburg, am Einfluß der Warthe in die Oder, 25 km nordöstl. von Frankfurt an der Oder).
Die preußische Besatzung (2.400 M. mit 92 Geschützen) unter Oberst v. Ingersleben ergibt sich ohne Schwertstreich an 1.500 Franzosen unter Brig.-Gen. Gauthier.
Die Besatzung wurde kriegsgefangen abgeführt, Offiziere auf Ehrenwort entlassen.
```

By Höpfner's account the summons, the threats and the dictated terms were the French commanders' own steps at Küstrin; the move on Küstrin was Davout's order (claim posture). Höpfner does not say which general dictated the terms. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'with the main body of the corps Marshal Davout set out on the 28th from the area in front of Berlin, and on the 29th detached from Müncheberg the division Güdin with 12 guns on Küstrin, to seize the bridgehead there if possible'; 'General Güdin summoned the fortress and let the commandant know that he would bombard the town if the surrender were refused'; 'in the night before 1 November General Güdin received the order to set out at once for the main body of the 3rd corps at Frankfurt, as Napoleon would set part of Marshal Augereau's troops marching to Küstrin and assign them to invest the fortress'; 'General Güdin had to comply with the order, set out at daybreak on 1 November, and left behind only the 85th infantry regiment under General Gauthier'; 'Lieutenant Thynkel believed he had to obey, met the first French post at the far end of the suburb, and was taken to General Petit, who was about to have the posts relieved'; 'the general seemed willing to enter into negotiations, but was prevented from it by Colonel Düplin of the 85th regiment, who was present and declared: if the town were not surrendered within 2 hours, the bombardment would begin'; 'the commandant was received on the other side by General Gauthier and Colonel Düplin; it was put to him that Stettin had fallen, the Hohenlohe corps was captured, Küstrin badly garrisoned, the bombardment would begin at once and not stop until the town had been reduced to ashes. The commandant'; 'the French general dictated the points of capitulation, by which at noon on 1 November the gates were to be occupied by 3 companies of French grenadiers, the garrison was to lay down its arms, safeguards were to be granted to the members of the Chamber and the property of the inhabitants protected. Lieutenant Thynkel refused his signature'; 'immediately after the signing the commandant crossed back over the Oder accompanied by Colonel Düplin and two soldiers, and in a short time the fortress was occupied by grenadiers crossing over'; 'Marshal Davout went at once in person to Küstrin, had the bridges restored and made all arrangements so that the following corps should profit from the unexpected conquest of a fortified place on the Oder, which together with Stettin offered an excellent base for the further operations against the Vistula' (OCR); the Bulletin, as in claim side-b-strength-french.",

      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: Colonel Ingersleben, the commandant, had been ordered on 17 October to make all defensive arrangements to secure the fortress against a forcible attack. In the fight at the bridgehead the Prussians escaped over the bridge he had already set on fire. That evening, when bugles sounded at the end of the Oder bridge, he told the engineer of the place, Lieutenant Thynkel, to go over and ask what the alarm meant and to threaten to burn the suburbs; when Thynkel objected to threatening or negotiating with the enemy, he sent the artillery lieutenant Wille to agree that if the enemy kept quiet he would not fire on the bridgehead. On the morning of 1 November he told his staff officers that he had sure news of a corps of 100,000 men approaching on the right bank, that no relief was to be expected and that the state of the garrison was known to all. Colonel Weyherr advised surrender rather than see the suburbs burned, Colonel Manteuffel agreed, trusting the commandant to act on his instructions, Colonel Boumann of the artillery said the commandant could do as he pleased, and Thynkel held that the fortress must and could defend itself, the main wall holding even without the outworks, and that a bombardment would not take it, the garrison having casemates. The commandant declared that he would not have the town burned and sent Thynkel to negotiate an armistice of 8 to 14 days; on Thynkel's report he said there was no time to lose and went himself, his wife's pleas being set aside by the Küstrin Kammerpräsident, who had gained great influence over him. Received by Gauthier and Düplin, he let himself be moved to capitulate, answering Thynkel's objections that he knew the Grand Duke of Berg was approaching with 100,000 men, after which no capitulation would be possible, and that he must not let the town be burned or its citizens made unhappy. Thynkel refused to sign. A court martial sentenced Ingersleben to be shot for proven cowardice; the King pardoned him to fortress imprisonment for life.",

    {
      "id": "capitulation",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Küstrin on 1 November: the Prussian garrison surrendered without striking a blow to the French under Gauthier and was led away as prisoners of war, the officers being released on parole. Höpfner dates it 1 November: by the terms the French general dictated, the gates were to be occupied at noon by 3 companies of French grenadiers, the garrison was to lay down its arms, the members of the Chamber were to be granted safeguards and the inhabitants' property protected; grenadiers crossing the Oder soon occupied the fortress, and the garrison, assembled in the market square, threw down its arms. The Emperor wrote on 2 November that Küstrin had surrendered the day before; the 25th Bulletin, that Davout had it invested and summoned and it surrendered, the officers returning home on parole and the soldiers being taken to France.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",

### B375d: KAPITULATION von Anklam (1./11. 1806)

Bodart entry: source `bodart-1908-transcription-v1`, section(s) p375, as printed:

```text
1806 1./11. KAPITULATION von Anklam
(Stadt in Preußen, Pommern, an der Peene, 75 km nordwestl. von Stettin).
Vor der französischen Dragonerbrigade Becker (ca. 1.000 M.) strecken 2.200 Preußen (1.100 Inft., 1.100 Kav.) unter Gen. v. Bila die Waffen, wonach die Mannschaften in Kriegsgefangenschaft gerieten, die Offiziere gegen Ehrenwort entlassen wurden.
```

      "id": "side-a-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Murat wrote that he had had Beker summon the enemy corps at Anklam while Lasalle pushed everything on the road from Stettin to Anklam before him, and that Beker reported he had carried out the order; Belliard told Beker to summon all troops he met, to make no more written capitulations, and to say only that the troops were prisoners of war to be sent to France, the officers keeping their horses and baggage, with Beker's good offices for their parole. Beker wrote from Cosenow on 30 October that, as the fog increased the darkness and the town was closed, he had halted there and would summon the officer commanding the troops at daybreak (OCR passage). On the 31st, by his own account, he observed the corps with General Boussard, had everything left on the left bank charged, took more than 300 cavalry and as many infantry in several attacks, and by multiplying demonstrations and summoning the general forced him to accept the capitulation, treating with 2 officers sent by Bila on Belliard's conditions; to Lasalle he wrote that after various attempts and partial captures he had entered into negotiations, whose outcome he did not yet know, the night hampering him (OCR passage). Höpfner has the French make as if to cross the Peene at Stolpe, without success, and send a parlementaire who demanded surrender because Stettin had capitulated. Murat gave Beker the greatest praise, writing that he had made Bila capitulate after a very vigorous charge in the town, and the 25th Bulletin and Dumas have him charge the column on the plain and enter the town with it; Belliard complimented him for the Prince on his fine expedition (OCR passage).",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "The French letters, the Bulletin and Höpfner, read from the page images, with the OCR passages marked. Beker's attacks, demonstrations and summons were his own steps at Anklam, made under Murat's order (claim posture). English renderings (ours): Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Friedland, 31 October 1806, 6 o'clock in the evening'; 'I had the honour to announce to you this morning that I was marching on Friedland, and that I would have summoned by General'; 'Beker the enemy corps that was at Anklam, while General Lasalle would push before him everything on the road from Stettin to Anklam, making for Stretense'; 'General Beker reports to me that he has indeed carried out my order, but that he has taken prisoner only the tail of this corps, the rest having crossed the Peene in the night and raised the drawbridge on him. 400 men have fallen into his power, of whom 260 mounted cuirassiers'; Belliard, 'General Belliard to General Beker. Pasewalk, 31 October 1806, 2 o'clock in the morning'; 'summon all the troops you meet to surrender; make no more capitulations in writing; say only that the troops are prisoners of war and sent back to France; that the officers keep their horses and baggage, and that you will use your good offices with the Prince for them to be prisoners of war on parole, which will surely not be refused them'; Beker, 'General Beker to the Grand Duke of Berg. Cosenow, 30 October 1806'; 'as the fog increases the darkness and the town is closed, I have halted at Cosenow, and tomorrow at daybreak I shall summon the officer commanding the troops to make them prisoners' (OCR); 'General Beker to the Grand Duke of Berg. Anklam, 31 October 1806'; 'having observed with General Boussard during the day a corps of 2,000 men who had taken refuge in Pomerania, having had'; 'everything that remained on the left bank of the river charged, and taken in various attacks more than 300 cavalry and as many infantry, I have succeeded, by multiplying my demonstrations and summoning the general to give himself up as a prisoner, in forcing him to accept the capitulation that has been customary in such circumstances'; 'at this moment 2 officers sent by General Bila are leaving here, with whom I have treated on the conditions prescribed by General Belliard. Thus tomorrow morning this column, 3,000 men strong, of whom 1,000 to 1,200 cavalry, and commanded by 2 generals, will lay down its arms and be directed on Friedland, where Your Highness will give it a destination, allowing the officers to retire to their homes with their baggage, to which they are infinitely attached'; 'General Beker to General Lasalle. Anklam,' (OCR); 'after making various attempts and partial captures, I have succeeded in entering into negotiations. The Frenchman called on the general to surrender, as Stettin had capitulated'; Murat, 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Friedland, 1 November 1806, half past 4 in the morning'; 'I hasten to announce to Your Majesty that the whole corps which I had been told had embarked at Anklam is in the power of your troops. He speaks very highly of General Boussart. We lost in this charge only an adjudant sous-officier and a few dragoons'; the Bulletin, '25th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 2 November 1806'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg had his headquarters on the 31st at Friedland. His dispositions made, he ordered the attack on the column of the Prussian general Bila, which General Beker charged, on the plain in front of the little town of Anklam, with General Boussart's dragoon brigade.       "id": "side-b-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: General Bila I, who reached Anklam at 10 in the evening, had the cash boxes and archives he had brought shipped to Usedom in the night before the 31st. On the morning of the 31st, with news of the enemy's approach growing, he had the troops fall in and sent the baggage to Pinnow to be ferried over before them; Major Nostitz went ahead to arrange the ferries, and the general left his brother to cross at Wolgast. He left Anklam at 7 in the morning and only then sent an orderly to Rittmeister Hiller at Görke to march through Anklam. As the enemy appeared, Captain Poyda with the rear guard barely had time to draw up the Peene bridge, and he held it until 5 in the evening while Bila I stood with the infantry behind the long Peene causeway between Ziethen and Relzow, meaning to march off to Pinnow in the night. When Captain Zimietzki's grenadier company relieved Poyda, its captain accepted a parlementaire and sent him to the general. Despairing of escape, though his brother had fully prepared him for Stettin's fall, and weighing the fatigue of men and horses, the idea that they could not live on Usedom and the town's request not to be ruined by a further defence, the general, in agreement with his brother, who had made no arrangements to cross at Lassahn or Wolgast, accepted the capitulation. Höpfner judges that it differed little from Pasewalk: the infantry had only 1½ miles to march to the Pinnow ferry and the cavalry 2½ to Lassahn and 3 to Wolgast, and the town's request made no sense.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 225-227 and 230. Höpfner does not name his sources for this passage. English renderings (ours): 'when General Bila I arrived at Anklam at 10 o'clock in the evening, he ordered that the grenadier battalion Sack and the company of Treuenfels should join his corps'; 'General Bila I had the cash boxes and archives he had brought embarked for Usedom that same night before the 31st under the lead of Captain Heyden, to go to Kolberg or Danzig'; 'after the union of the two generals Bila had thus taken place, and the news of the enemy's approach had increased, General Bila I had the troops present in Anklam fall in on the morning of the 31st, but sent the baggage off to Pinnow, so that it would be across before the troops arrived'; 'Major Nostitz of vac. Grävenitz went ahead to set up the ferrying. The general left it to his brother to cross the Peene at Wolgast and to send an officer ahead there as well'; 'at 7 o'clock in the morning General Bila I left Anklam and only now sent an orderly to Rittmeister Hiller at Görke with the order to march through Anklam'; 'at this moment, however, the enemy also appeared before Anklam, and Captain Poyda with the rear guard left behind in the town barely had time to draw up the Peene bridge'; 'it was the dragoon brigade Becker that appeared before the two generals Bila. As the French had no'; 'guns with them, Captain Poyda defended the Peene bridge steadfastly, while General Bila I stood with the infantry behind the long Peene causeway between Ziethen and Relzow'; 'the general intended to march off to Pinnow in the night, and would probably have carried out this intention undisturbed, had misfortune not brought him a parlementaire'; 'until 5 o'clock in the evening Captain Poyda had held his ground at the Peene bridge, when he was relieved there by the grenadier company of Captain Zimietzki'; as in claim side-a-command for the parlementaire; 'although the general had been fully prepared for this event by his brother, he nevertheless despaired of escaping with his troops, as the French could always forestall him again from Stettin'; 'as there was added to this the fatigue of men and horses, the idea of not being able to live on the island of Usedom, and the request of the town of Anklam not to ruin it by a further defence of the Peene, the general, in agreement with his brother, who had made no arrangements at all to cross the Peene at Lassahn or Wolgast, accepted the capitulation, and surrendered to the enemy with 1100 men of infantry and 1073 horses on 1 November'; 'this capitulation differs little from the one at Pasewalk. The fall of Stettin could not take from General Bila the hope of still escaping; in the worst case there remained to him the attempt to embark at Swinemünde'; 'the fatigue of men and horses may have been very great, but the infantry had probably already recovered somewhat, and had only a march of 1½ miles to the Pinnow ferry, the cavalry 2½ to Lassahn and 3 miles to Wolgast, where they could have crossed at all leisure if a small part had been sacrificed at the Peene bridge at Anklam'; 'the request of the town of Anklam made no sense at all; the musketry at the bridge could not possibly do it particular harm, and to escape the tumult such a fight causes, one cannot after all ask a couple of thousand men to submit to the disgrace of a capitulation'.",

      "dimension": "information",
      "value": "Lasalle wrote on 30 October, citing a postillon who had left Anklam the previous evening, of a corps of guards du corps, green hussars, cuirassiers and dragoons, with many infantry and much baggage and no guns, its commander unknown, put at 6,000 men, with detachments arriving every day. Beker approached Anklam on the evening of the 30th to reconnoitre the bivouac fires on the Stettin road, found the point guarded by a picket of hussars backed by infantry, and heard from peasants and a postillon that the town was crowded with fugitives from every regiment; he would summon the officer commanding the troops at daybreak, who, he wrote, did not know how near the French were or where to retreat, since Beker was certain that the Swedes refused to receive them in Pomerania, except their baggage (OCR passages). On 31 October Beker wrote that he was certain Blücher had recrossed the Oder 5 days before. After the capitulation an order from Friedland for chef d'escadron Boyer found it astonishing that no one could yet say whether the corps that had capitulated belonged to Blücher's or Hohenlohe's column (OCR passage).",

The bridge of Anklam is cut on the side of Sweden. This corps is put at 6,000 men; it comes from Mecklenburg and detachments of it arrive every day'; Beker, as in claim side-a-command for the heading of 30 October; 'I approached the town of Anklam at 8 o'clock in the evening to reconnoitre the bivouac fires set up on the Stettin road; the point I made for was guarded by a picket of hussars supported by infantry; and some peasants, as well as a postillon, who had come out of the town, assured me that it was crowded with fugitives from all the regiments, without being able to answer the questions about the march of General Blücher'; as in claim side-a-command for the fog (OCR); 'he does not know how near the French troops are and does not know besides where to retreat, since I am certain that the Swedes refuse to receive them in Pomerania, except the baggage, which has already been sent into the interior of Pomerania both from Mecklenburg and from Anklam' (OCR); Beker, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading of 31 October; 'I am certain that General Blücher recrossed the Oder 5 days ago with 2 regiments of cavalry and some artillery'; the order, 'order for chef d'escadron Boyer. After the surrender Murat charged Beker with taking the corps to Spandau with Boussart's brigade and with claiming the treasure, a few leagues from Anklam in the interior of Pomerania, from the authorities of the country, and ordered him to disarm the cavalry but lead its regiments mounted to Potsdam so as to keep 1,400 or 1,500 horses.",
