      "id": "side-a-strength",
      "dimension": "strength",
      "value": "Side A (French): Bodart gives 16,000 men under Marshal Ney. Höpfner: Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 cavalry at its disposal. Ney's order for the passage of the Elbe of 23 October names the 3rd division, the army's park and the headquarters baggage, General Klein's 2 dragoon regiments, the 76th and 69th regiments with the 2nd division's artillery and baggage, the 39th, the 10th chasseurs and the 6th light. On 25 October Ney wrote that Vandamme had taken command of the 3rd division; that Klein had only 2 dragoon regiments, the 1st and the 14th, together 700 mounted men, having detached 3 regiments to Nordhausen by the Grand Duke's order; that the 10th chasseurs had at most 200 horses and the 3rd hussars had stayed at Erfurt; and that escorts for prisoners and deserters greatly reduced his cavalry; he asked for one more regiment of light cavalry out of the most pressing need. On 3 November he wrote that by the major general's orders he had redirected the 2 dragoon regiments to Berlin, Klein going to rejoin General Picard's brigade and go to Berlin with his division; that Vandamme's division was absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks; that on the right bank there was not a quarter of the troops needed; and that the whole of his troops was not too numerous for the blockade. For the raid of the night of 31 October to 1 November Ney's daily report gives General Colbert 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, and Höpfner gives General Kolbert 600 light infantry, 2 voltigeur companies and 2 squadrons; both place 6 grenadier companies at Schönebeck. On 8 November Ney wrote that a detachment of the 3rd hussars, some voltigeur companies and a grenadier battalion of his corps were being sent from Erfurt, to arrive on the 13th, and that the rest of the voltigeurs and hussars used to escort the prisoners would leave Erfurt on the 8th. No passage read gives a count of side A's infantry or a total for Ney's corps.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "inherited",
      "rationale": "Bodart from the frame transcription; Höpfner, Ney's letters and his daily report read from the page images, the figures checked on full-resolution crops. The corps was brought to Magdeburg before the investment, and its cavalry was reduced by orders from above (the Grand Duke's detachment to Nordhausen, the major general's order sending the dragoons to Berlin), so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner's 900 cavalry equal Ney's 700 dragoons and 200 chasseurs of 25 October (our arithmetic); whether he took them from Ney's letter is not shown, and by 3 November the dragoons had been sent away. Whether the light cavalry regiment Ney asked for was sent is not shown. The daily report is Ney's: his signature closes it on p. 645. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 men of cavalry at its disposal, but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'the passage will take place in the following manner'; 'the 3rd division will open the march; then the army's park and the headquarters baggage; General Klein's 2 dragoon regiments; the 76th and 69th regiments, the artillery and the baggage of the 2nd division; the 39th and the 10th chasseurs. The march will be closed by the 6th light'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 25 October 1806'; 'General Vandamme has arrived at the army corps and taken command of the 3rd division'; 'General Klein is also with me; but he has only 2 dragoon regiments, the 1st and the 14th, making together 700 mounted men. This general has detached 3 regiments to Nordhausen to scour the country and gather up escaped prisoners. This disposition was ordered by the Grand Duke'; 'the 10th chasseurs has at most 200 horses, and the 3rd hussars stayed at Erfurt to escort the prisoners'; 'convoys of prisoners and deserters, which reach me every day, require escorts that greatly reduce my cavalry'; 'I beg Your Highness to have one more regiment of light cavalry sent to me, if possible. This request is prompted by the most pressing need'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'in accordance with your orders, I have changed the direction of the 2 dragoon regiments that spent last night at Nedlitz, on the Brandenburg road, to go to Berlin'; 'General Picard's brigade must have crossed the Elbe today at Dessau; I have'; 'informed General Klein of it, who answered me that he would rejoin that brigade and go to Berlin with his division united'; 'General Vandamme's division is absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks of the Elbe, the extent of the fortifications being immense. I have gone over all the positions that it is indispensable to occupy: those of the right bank require fewer men, yet there is not a quarter of the troops needed at that point; and in case of a sortie General Colbert would be forced to fall back on Pechau and Gommern while awaiting the help I would send him from the 2nd division'; 'this work, on which the engineer officers have been busy for 4 days, will prove to Your Highness that the whole of the troops is not too numerous to blockade a place that holds many more men than is believed and that must be watched very closely, to deprive it of the resources in subsistence it could draw from its surroundings'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; '6 companies of grenadiers are at Schönebeck to guard the bridge over the Elbe and ready to support General Colbert's troops in case of a sortie'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; '6 companies of grenadiers served as bridge guard at Schönebeck and at the same time as the nearest support of General Kolbert'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönebeck, 8 November 1806'; 'General Thouvenot informs me from Erfurt that he is sending me at Schönbeck a detachment of the 3rd hussars, some companies of voltigeurs and a battalion of grenadiers of my army corps. This force will arrive on the 13th'; 'the rest of the voltigeurs and hussars who had been employed in escorting the prisoners will likewise leave Erfurt on the 8th for Schönbeck'.",

    {
      "id": "side-a-command",
      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner and Ney's letters: on 23 October Ney had a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck, to cross the Elbe and seize all the communications reaching Magdeburg on the right bank, and summoned the governor, who refused. When Soult left for Tangermünde, Ney relieved the 4th corps's posts before Magdeburg on the left bank and wrote on 25 October that General Colbert's light troops would cross the Elbe at Schönebeck the next day to form the investment on the right bank; Höpfner has him move his headquarters to Schönebeck and complete the investment on the right bank on the 27th, though still at a great distance from the place. By Ney's daily report of 2 November his troops drove the enemy's advanced posts under the cannon of the place from the 26th to the 28th, completing the blockade; Vandamme had some thirty shells fired into the town in the night of the 29th, which did not set it on fire (Höpfner: some shells, which did not set it alight); small posts were carried on the 30th and 31st; in the night of 31 October to 1 November Colbert surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester at 3 in the morning and set fire to the farms holding produce, Marchand had a post of 15 grenadiers carried, and a general reconnaissance went up to the ditches of the place; and, Ney wrote, the alarms he gave from time to time would tire the garrison still more. Höpfner has Kolbert drive the Prussian outposts into the fortress and the French posts pushed to 12—1500 paces from the glacis. Ney had the orders of the day announcing the capture of Prince Hohenlohe's corps and the surrender of Stettin spread in the town, and, by Höpfner, sent the governor the French Bulletin containing the capitulation of Prenzlau. He asked for mortars on 30 October, and the 4 he had asked of General Clarke arrived on 2 November. On 7 November he reported his troops and outposts entrenched, communications cut, his artillery placed to sweep the plain, and fire almost every night and signal rockets twice each night, alarms that exhausted the garrison. In the night of 4 to 5 November 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place (Höpfner and Ney), burning one house in the town and 2 in the Neustadt suburb (Ney). Ney made his last summons on the 5th, saying, by Höpfner, that the bombardment had only been meant to prove that he had the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes. On 6 November he sent his aide-de-camp Liger-Belair and Captain Regnard into Magdeburg with Major Wedell (Höpfner); by Ney's letters the parleys began on the 6th, he sent a draft capitulation on the 7th, Liger-Belair and Regnard signed the armistice of 7 November for side A, and he cut short the delay the governor asked for, so that the garrison would defile on the 11th. The capitulation was agreed in Ney's name by General of Brigade Dutaillis, chief of the general staff of the 6th corps, with Colonel Ligor-Belair and Captain Regnard (Höpfner's Dütaillis came into the fortress on the afternoon of the 8th), and signed, Ney wrote, on the evening of the 8th.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Höpfner, Ney's letters, his daily report and the armistice and capitulation texts, read from the page images. These were the steps of side A's commander and his generals at Magdeburg, so the claim is tagged commander-created; the bridge over the Elbe was also the major general's order, which Ney says on 3 November had been renewed (claim posture). Höpfner gives Ney's efforts to obtain mortars from Ney's correspondence captured at Gutstadt in 1807 (his footnote). Höpfner has Kolbert drive the outposts into the fortress; Ney's report says the enemy had withdrawn its small posts the night before. English renderings (ours): 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'I have the honour to report to Your Highness that I am having a bridge of boats built at Schönebeck; as soon as this operation is finished, I shall cross the Elbe to seize on the right bank of that river all the communications that lead to Magdeburg'; 'I have had Lieutenant General de Kleist, governor of Magdeburg, summoned; his answer was negative'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 25 October 1806'; 'Marshal Soult set out this morning with his army corps in the direction of Tangermünde; the aim of this movement is to close the passage of the Elbe to the Duke of Weimar'; 'I have accordingly had all the posts that the 4th corps held before Magdeburg on the left bank of the Elbe relieved'; 'a corps of light troops under General Colbert will cross the Elbe tomorrow at Schönebeck to form the investment of Magdeburg on the right bank of that river'; 'on 23 October Marshal Ney, whose headquarters had until then been at Groß-Ottersleben, had a bridge of boats thrown over the Elbe at Schönebeck, which was passable on the 25th'; 'Marshal Soult's departure for Tangermünde allowed only an observation of the fortress, for which Marshal Ney moved his headquarters to Schönebeck'; 'only on the 27th did he complete the investment on the right bank of the Elbe, though still at a great distance from the place'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the 26th, 27th and 28th were spent compelling the enemy's advanced posts on both banks of the Elbe to withdraw immediately under the cannon of the place; from then on the blockade was complete'; 'in the night of the 29th General Vandamme had some thirty shells fired, which fell in the town without setting it on fire. The enemy replied with his heavy artillery, but without any effect'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'did not interfere; in general it had so far come only to insignificant engagements'; 'in the same night General Vandamme had some shells thrown at the town, which, however, did not set it alight'; 'the 30th and the 31st were spent carrying some small enemy posts; some thirty men were taken, and as many killed or wounded. We had 2 men killed and 3 wounded'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; 'this operation took place at 3 in the morning; the enemy had withdrawn all his small forward posts during the night before. Fire was set to all the farms that'; 'held produce, so that the enemy can no longer draw any help from them'; 'in the same night of the 31st to 1 November General Marchand had an enemy post of 15 grenadiers, furnished by that of the Closterberg, carried; the enemy also had 4 killed and 6 wounded. We had neither killed nor wounded'; 'a general reconnaissance combined with General Vandamme's troops took place that same night along the whole length of the blockade line on the left bank of the Elbe and up to the ditches of the place. Its main object was to carry posts, but the enemy had taken the precaution of withdrawing them at the evening gun. The musketry was fairly brisk; we had neither killed nor wounded'; 'it is known that the garrison is tired of its service; it will be still more so through the alarms that we give it from time to time'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; 'the French posts on the right bank were now pushed forward to a distance of 12—1500 paces from the glacis, the supports in Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau, reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern'; 'Marshal Ney sent the governor of Magdeburg, through the former Rittmeister Willisen, burgomaster of Staßfurth, the French Bulletin that contained the capitulation of Prenzlau, and had the impossibility of a relief represented to him'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'I had the honour of writing to you on 30 October and asking you for some mortars to bombard Magdeburg; it would be all the more essential for me to have them at my disposal as the persons with whom I have intelligences in the place are only waiting for the moment when I have had bombs thrown, to force the governor, Count Kleist, to capitulate'; 'I have taken care to have the orders of the day announcing the capture of Prince Hohenlohe's army corps, the surrender of Stettin, etc., brought into the town and spread there'; 'P.S. — The 4 mortars I asked General Clarke for have just reached me this instant with their supply'; 'taken from the correspondence of Marshal Ney to Napoleon intercepted at Gutstadt in 1807, from which it also appears that the marshal made every arrangement to see some mortars brought before Magdeburg as quickly as possible'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'the troops are entrenched in their positions, as are the advanced posts: cuts have been made on various communications that the number of my troops did not allow me to guard: the artillery is placed on the flank and on the front of the divisions to sweep the plain and protect the withdrawal of the outposts in case of a sortie; in short, every measure has been taken to cut the enemy off from all communication with the outside and to take from him the means of foraging'; 'musketry and cannonade are repeated almost every night between Neustadt and Diesdorf, which tired the garrison of Magdeburg extremely. I have signal rockets fired twice each'; 'night. All these alarms exhaust the enemy, so that the deserters and prisoners say that the garrison has only one night of rest, during which it is often obliged to take up arms'; 'on the 5th I made my last summons to the governor, and on the 6th the parleys began. I have today sent a draft capitulation; M. de Kleist has assembled his council of war; it seems that opinions there are divided; but despite the delays this causes, I hope to have a definite answer shortly'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'in the night of the 4th to the 5th the 2nd division took up arms. The 3rd division was also under arms all night; the enemy attempted a sortie between 8 and 9 o'clock; he was sharply repulsed. 12 bombs and some shells were fired on the place; one house was burned in the town and 2 others in the suburb of Neustadt'; 'on 4 November the enemy attacked the Neustadt but was repulsed, and in the night to the 5th Marshal Ney had 12 bombs and also some shells thrown at the Altstadt and the Neustadt from the 4 mortars brought up meanwhile from Erfurt, and had the Neustadt attacked repeatedly in vain'; 'on the afternoon of the 5th Marshal Ney summoned the fortress again, with the remark that by the bombardment he had only wanted to prove that he possessed the means to reduce Magdeburg to ashes; at the same time he again recalled the misfortunes of the Prussian army and the impossibility of a relief, and asked the governor to have regard for the unfortunate 25,000 inhabitants, who would be exposed to the misfortune of a bombardment to no benefit for the state' (pp. 333-334); 'on 6 November the marshal sent his aide-de-camp Liger-Belair and Captain Regnard to Magdeburg, accompanied by Major Wedell of the Leib-Kürassier regiment, who had been taken prisoner at Prenzlau'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönebeck, 8 November 1806'; 'I have the honour to lay before Your Majesty a copy of the armistice concluded last night with the governor of Magdeburg'; 'I have at this moment officers in the place who are settling the conditions of the capitulation on the basis already agreed, that the garrison will be prisoner and sent to France, except the officers, who will return home on parole'; 'the governor asked for a delay for his arrangements; I have shortened it, and it will defile on the 11th'; 'done in duplicate at Magdeburg, 7 November 1806'; 'the adjutant-commandant, chief of staff of the advance guard of the 6th corps of the Grande Armée, Liger-Belair'; 'the captain aide-de-camp of His Excellency Marshal Ney, Regnard'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönbeck, 8 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'the fortress of Magdeburg surrenders to Your Majesty's arms; the capitulation was signed this evening; I have the honour to lay it before you'; 'articles of capitulation for the town and fortress of Magdeburg, agreed between General of Brigade Dutaillis, one of the commanders of the Legion of Honour, knight of the military order of Bavaria, and chief of the general staff of the 6th corps of the French Grande Armée in Germany (the'; 'Colonel Ligor-Belair and Captain Regnard), etc., stipulating in the name of Marshal of the Empire Ney'; 'on the 8th General Dütaillis, chief of staff of Marshal Ney, came into the fortress in the afternoon, and at 1 o'clock the capitulation was concluded'.",
      "citations": [

          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p347-figures-v1",
          "section": "p347",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 347 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "LE MARÉCHAL NEY AU MAJOR GÉNÉRAL.\n\nSchönebeck, 25 octobre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p347-figures-v1",
          "section": "p347",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 347 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "M. le maréchal Soult s'est mis en marche ce matin avec son corps d'armée sur la direction de Tangermünde; le but de ce mouvement est de fermer le passage de l'Elbe au duc de Weimar."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p347-figures-v1",
          "section": "p347",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 347 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "J'ai en conséquence fait relever tous les postes que le 4e corps occupait devant Magdeburg sur la rive gauche de l'Elbe."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p347-figures-v1",
          "section": "p347",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 347 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Un corps de troupes légères aux ordres du général Colbert passera demain l'Elbe à Schönebeck pour former l'investissement de Magdeburg sur la rive droite de ce fleuve."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p332-figures-v1",
          "section": "p332",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 332 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Am 23. Oktober ließ der M. Ney, dessen Hauptquartier bis dahin in Groß-Ottersleben gewesen, bei Schönebeck eine Schiffbrücke über die Elbe schlagen, welche am 25. passirbar war."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p332-figures-v1",
          "section": "p332",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 332 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Der Abmarsch des M. Soult auf Tangermünde gestattete lediglich eine Beobachtung der Festung, wozu der M. Ney sein Hauptquartier nach Schönebeck verlegte."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p332-figures-v1",
          "section": "p332",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 332 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Erst am 27. vollendete er die Einschließung auf dem rechten Elbufer, obgleich immer noch in weiter Entfernung vom Platz."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p644-figures-v1",
          "section": "p644",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 644 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "RAPPORT JOURNALIER SUR LE BLOCUS DE MAGDEBURG.\n\nSchönebeck, 2 novembre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p645-figures-v1",
          "section": "p645",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 645 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Mal NEY."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p644-figures-v1",
          "section": "p644",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 644 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Les 26, 27 et 28 ont été employés à contraindre les postes avancés de l'ennemi sur les 2 rives de l'Elbe à se retirer immédiatement sous le canon de la place; dès lors le blocus a été complet."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p644-figures-v1",
          "section": "p644",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 644 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Dans la nuit du 29 le général Vandamme a fait tirer une trentaine d'obus qui sont tombés dans la ville sans y mettre le feu. L'ennemi a répondu avec sa grosse artillerie, mais sans aucun effet."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p332-figures-v1",
          "section": "p332",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 332 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Am 29. fing man an einige Gebäude wegbrechen zu lassen, welche der Vertheidigung der Sudenburg und Neustadt hinderlich waren; der Rest wurde in der Nacht niedergebrannt. Der Feind"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p333-figures-v1",
          "section": "p333",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 333 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "störte nicht; überhaupt war es bis dahin nur zu unbedeutenden Gefechten gekommen."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p333-figures-v1",
          "section": "p333",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 333 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "In derselben Nacht ließ der General Vandamme einige Granaten nach der Stadt werfen, die indessen nicht zündeten."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p644-figures-v1",
          "section": "p644",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 644 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Le 30 et le 31 ont été employés à enlever quelques petits postes ennemis; on a pris une trentaine d'hommes, tué ou blessé le même nombre. Nous avons eu 2 hommes tués et 3 blessés."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p644-figures-v1",
          "section": "p644",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 644 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Dans la nuit du 31 au 1er novembre, le général Colbert avec 600 hommes du 6e léger, 2 compagnies de voltigeurs du 39e, soutenu par 1 escadron de hussards et de chasseurs et 2 pièces de 4, s'est approché de Friedrichstadt, hors de la portée du canon, a enveloppé les villages de Crakau et de Prester, de même que toutes les fermes plus rapprochées de la place."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p644-figures-v1",
          "section": "p644",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 644 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Cette opération a eu lieu à 3 heures du matin; l'ennemi avait retiré la veille pendant la nuit tous ses petits postes antérieurs. Le feu a été mis à toutes les fermes qui"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p645-figures-v1",
          "section": "p645",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 645 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "renfermaient des denrées, en sorte que l'ennemi ne peut plus en tirer aucun secours."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p645-figures-v1",
          "section": "p645",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 645 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Dans cette même nuit du 31 au 1er novembre, le général Marchand a fait enlever un poste ennemi de 15 grenadiers, fourni par celui de Closterberg; l'ennemi a eu en outre 4 tués et 6 blessés. Nous n'avons eu ni tués ni blessés."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p645-figures-v1",
          "section": "p645",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 645 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Une reconnaissance générale combinée avec les troupes du général Vandamme a eu lieu cette même nuit sur tout le développement de la ligne de blocus sur la rive gauche de l'Elbe et jusqu'aux fossés de la place. L'objet principal était d'enlever des postes, mais l'ennemi avait eu la précaution de les faire rentrer au coup de canon de retraite. La fusillade a été assez vive; nous n'avons eu ni tués ni blessés."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p645-figures-v1",
          "section": "p645",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 645 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "On sait que la garnison est fatiguée de service; elle le sera encore davantage par les alertes que nous lui donnons de temps à autre."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p333-figures-v1",
          "section": "p333",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 333 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Der General Kolbert, der auf dem rechten Ufer kommandirte, sammelte in der folgenden Nacht 600 Mann leichter Infanterie, 2 Kompagnien Voltigeurs und 2 Schwadronen und griff um 3 Uhr Morgens des 1. Novembers die preußischen Vorposten an, trieb sie in die Festung zurück und zündete die Dörfer Krakau und Prester an."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p333-figures-v1",
          "section": "p333",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 333 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Die französischen Posten wurden nunmehr auf dem rechten Ufer auf 12—1500 Schritt Entfernung vom Glacis vorgeschoben, die Soutiens in Biederitz, Alt- und Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs und Pechau, Reserven zu Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz und Gommern."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p333-figures-v1",
          "section": "p333",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 333 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Dem Gouverneur von Magdeburg sandte der M. Ney durch den ehemaligen Rittmeister Willisen, Bürgermeister von Staßfurth,¹) das französische Bülletin, welches die Kapitulation von Prenzlau enthielt, und ließ ihm die Unmöglichkeit eines Entsatzes vorstellig machen."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p642-figures-v1",
          "section": "p642",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 642 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "LE MARÉCHAL NEY AU MAJOR GÉNÉRAL.\n\nSchönebeck, 2 novembre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p642-figures-v1",
          "section": "p642",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 642 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "J'ai eu l'honneur de vous écrire le 30 octobre et de vous demander quelques mortiers pour bombarder Magdeburg; il serait d'autant plus essentiel que j'en eusse à ma disposition que les personnes avec lesquelles j'ai des intelligences dans la place n'attendent que le moment où j'aurai fait lancer des bombes pour forcer le gouverneur, comte de Kleist, à capituler."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p643-figures-v1",
          "section": "p643",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 643 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "J'ai eu soin de faire entrer et répandre dans la ville les ordres du jour qui annoncent la prise du corps d'armée du prince de Hohenlohe, la reddition de Stettin, etc."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p643-figures-v1",
          "section": "p643",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 643 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "P.-S. — Les 4 mortiers que j'ai demandés au général Clarke viennent de m'arriver dans l'instant avec leur approvisionnement."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p331-figures-v1",
          "section": "p331",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 331 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "1) Aus der im Jahre 1807 bei Gutstadt aufgefangenen Korrespondenz des M. Ney an Napoleon entnommen, aus der auch hervorgeht, daß der Marschall alle Veranstaltungen traf, um schleunigst einige Mörser vor Magdeburg geschafft zu sehen."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p764-figures-v1",
          "section": "p764",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 764 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "LE MARÉCHAL NEY AU MAJOR GÉNÉRAL.\n\nSchönebeck, 7 novembre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p764-figures-v1",
          "section": "p764",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 764 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Les troupes sont retranchées dans leurs positions, de même que les postes avancés : des coupures ont été faites sur différentes communications que le nombre de mes troupes ne me permettait pas de garder : l'artillerie est disposée sur le flanc et sur le front des divisions pour battre la plaine et protéger la retraite des avant-postes en cas de sortie; enfin toutes les mesures ont été prises pour ôter à l'ennemi toute communication avec ses dehors et lui enlever les moyens de fourrager."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p764-figures-v1",
          "section": "p764",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 764 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "La fusillade et la canonnade se répètent presque toutes les nuits entre Neustadt et Diesdorf, ce qui fatiguait extrêmement la garnison de Magdeburg. Je fais tirer 2 fois chaque"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p765-figures-v1",
          "section": "p765",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 765 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "nuit des fusées de signaux. Toutes ces alertes excèdent l'ennemi en sorte que les déserteurs et prisonniers disent que la garnison n'a qu'une nuit de repos pendant laquelle elle est souvent obligée de prendre les armes."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p765-figures-v1",
          "section": "p765",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 765 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Le 5 j'ai fait ma dernière sommation au gouverneur et le 6 les pourparlers ont commencé. J'ai envoyé aujourd'hui un projet de capitulation; M. de Kleist a fait assembler son conseil de guerre; il paraît qu'il y règne de la diversité dans les opinions; mais malgré les lenteurs que cela cause, j'espère avoir dans peu une réponse définitive."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p765-figures-v1",
          "section": "p765",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 765 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "LE MARÉCHAL NEY AU MAJOR GÉNÉRAL.\n\nSchönebeck, 7 novembre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p765-figures-v1",
          "section": "p765",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 765 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "La nuit du 4 au 5 la 2e division a pris les armes. La 3e division a également été sous les armes toute la nuit; l'ennemi a tenté une sortie entre 8 et 9 heures; il a été vivement repoussé. On a tiré sur la place 12 bombes et quelques obus; une maison a été brûlée dans la ville et 2 autres dans le faubourg de Neustadt."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p333-figures-v1",
          "section": "p333",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 333 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Am 4. November griff der Feind die Neustadt an, wurde indessen zurückgewiesen, und in der Nacht zum 5. ließ der M. Ney aus den mittlerweile von Erfurt herbeigezogenen 4 Mörsern 12 Bomben und außerdem einige Granaten nach der Alt- und Neustadt werfen und die Neustadt wiederholentlich vergeblich angreifen."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p333-figures-v1",
          "section": "p333",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 333 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Am 5. Nachmittags forderte der M. Ney die Festung abermals auf, mit der Bemerkung, daß er durch das Bombardement nur habe beweisen wollen, daß er die Mittel besitze, Magdeburg"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p334-figures-v1",
          "section": "p334",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 334 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "einzuäschern; zugleich brachte er nochmals die Unfälle der preußischen Armee und die Unmöglichkeit eines Entsatzes in Erinnerung und bat den Gouverneur, auf die unglücklichen 25,000 Einwohner Rücksicht zu nehmen, welche ohne Frommen für den Staat dem Unglück eines Bombardements ausgesetzt würden."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "hoepfner-1855-bd2-p334-figures-v1",
          "section": "p334",
          "locator": "Höpfner, Der Krieg von 1806 und 1807, Bd. 2 (2nd ed., 1855), p. 334 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Am 6. November sandte der Marschall seinen Adjutanten Liger-Belair und den Kapitain Regnard nach Magdeburg, in Begleitung des Majors Wedell vom Leib-Kürassier-Regmt., der bei Prenzlau gefangen genommen war."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p787-figures-v1",
          "section": "p787",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 787 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "LE MARÉCHAL NEY A L'EMPEREUR.\n\nSchönebeck, 8 novembre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p787-figures-v1",
          "section": "p787",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 787 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "J'ai l'honneur de mettre sous les yeux de V. M. copie de l'armistice conclu la nuit dernière avec le gouverneur de Magdeburg²."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p788-figures-v1",
          "section": "p788",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 788 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "J'ai dans ce moment dans la place des officiers qui règlent les conditions de la capitulation sur cette base déjà consentie que la garnison sera prisonnière et envoyée en France à l'exception des officiers qui rentreront chez eux sur parole."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p788-figures-v1",
          "section": "p788",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 788 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Le gouverneur demandait un délai pour ses dispositions; je l'ai restreint et il défilera le 11."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p788-figures-v1",
          "section": "p788",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 788 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Fait double à Magdeburg, le 7 novembre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p788-figures-v1",
          "section": "p788",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 788 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "L'adjudant commandant, chef de l'état-major de l'avant-garde du 6e corps de la Grande Armée,\n\nLIGER-BELAIR,"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p788-figures-v1",
          "section": "p788",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 788 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "Le capitaine aide de camp de S. Exc. M. le maréchal Ney,\n\nREGNARD,"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p789-figures-v1",
          "section": "p789",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 789 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "LE MARÉCHAL NEY A L'EMPEREUR.\n\nSchönbeck, 8 novembre 1806."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p789-figures-v1",
          "section": "p789",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 789 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "La forteresse de Magdeburg se rend aux armes de V. M.; la capitulation¹ a été signée ce soir; j'ai l'honneur de vous la mettre sous les yeux."
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p789-figures-v1",
          "section": "p789",
          "locator": "Foucart, Campagne de Prusse (1806): Prenzlow - Lubeck (1890), p. 789 (transcribed from the page image)",
          "quote": "1. Articles de capitulation pour la ville et forteresse de Magdeburg, convenus entre MM. le général de brigade Dutaillis, l'un des commandants de la Légion d'honneur, chevalier de l'ordre militaire de Bavière, et chef de l'état-major général du 6e corps de la Grande Armée française en Allemagne (le"
        },
        {
          "source_id": "foucart-prusse-1890-t2-p790-figures-v1",

      "dimension": "responsibility",
      "value": "Höpfner: the governor, General of Infantry von Kleist, was 73 and deprived of the use of part of his limbs by age, illness, wounds and the hardships of war; after ordering everything himself by day and night in the first days he collapsed into slackness, and he had turned his confidence chiefly to General Count Wartensleben, who seems to have wished early on for a speedy surrender and, by Ney's report, is said to have told the French parlementaire on 23 October to throw bombs and shells into the town to change the governor's mind. Ney's letter of 23 October has Wartensleben tell adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to bring the governor to reason if a few shells were fired on the place. The commandant, Colonel dü Trossel, stood in complete dependence on the governor and was seldom told of negotiations or orders. Kleist had neglected to supply the fortress with fresh meat and other provisions from the right bank in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October, for which, Höpfner says, the confusion in the fortress until the Hohenlohe troops had left may at first have been to blame, and he had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence. He refused Ney's summons of 23 October, giving his word, Ney wrote, not to thwart French movements out of range of his cannon, and asked on the 27th for a meeting, held with Vandamme on the 28th without result. On the 29th the defenders began to pull down buildings that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and Neustadt and burned the rest in the night, and on the 31st the garrison foraged along the right bank (Höpfner; Ney's report gives a sortie of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns, which carried off 6 wagons of forage). Kleist asked Ney to let an officer go to Berlin to learn the situation of the Prussian army, proposing a cessation of arms until the officer's return, but did not accept Ney's condition that the town surrender once it was proved that no Prussian army remained (Ney, 2 and 3 November; Höpfner gives the request as his answer to the summons of the 5th). On 6 November he assembled the generals present and the commandant, laid the correspondence with Ney before them, had Major Wedell give an account of the army's march to the Oder and announced his decision to capitulate; he asked no advice, curtly rejected all objections, silencing Major General v. Alvensleben, who asked what they had been called for and said that they still lacked nothing, and formally ordered the meeting to sign the protocol. Höpfner writes that a formal council of war, to which by regulation all the garrison's staff officers had to be called, was rightly expected to follow, and that the negotiations went on; neither the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, nor the artillery officer of the place, Major Hüser, was called to the conference. When the engineer represented that the fortress could hold 4—5 weeks after the opening of the trenches, Kleist answered that Wedell had convinced him that relief was hopeless and that he must capitulate out of humanity. All the generals except Wartensleben had shown themselves more or less averse to surrender. The armistice of 7 November was signed for side B by Colonel du Troussel and Captain Le Blanc (Foucart's text; Höpfner names General Renouard, dü Trossel and Leblank), and the capitulation was agreed in Kleist's name by Major General de Renouard with du Troussel and Leblanc. Ney wrote on 7 November that Kleist had assembled his council of war, where opinions seemed divided, and on 8 November that the governor raised difficulties up to the signing, the magistrates and inhabitants wishing to capitulate and the officers insisting on resistance. The 29th Bulletin says that when several houses had been burned in the bombardment the inhabitants showed their discontent and the commandant asked to capitulate.",

      "phase": "commander_created",
      "rationale": "Side B's history, read from the page images of pp. 331-335, with Ney's letters, his daily report, the armistice and capitulation texts and the 29th Bulletin from the page images. These were the governor's decisions at Magdeburg, so the claim is tagged commander-created. Höpfner takes Wartensleben's words from Ney's report to Napoleon, from the correspondence captured at Gutstadt in 1807 (his footnote), and in this section cites the records of the inquiry into the capitulation (claim side-b-information). The armistice Foucart prints is signed for side B by du Troussel and Le Blanc only; Höpfner adds Renouard, who in Foucart's text heads side B's agents for the capitulation. The Bulletin's 'commandant' is not named in the passage read; Höpfner gives that title to dü Trossel and calls Kleist the governor. Höpfner's account of the meeting of 6 November and Ney's mention of a council of war on the 7th are kept as given; the passages read do not show whether they describe one meeting. English renderings (ours): 'governor of Magdeburg was the General of Infantry von Kleist, an old man of 73, who had greatly distinguished himself in earlier wars, especially at the siege of Mainz, but was now deprived of the use of part of his limbs by age, illness, wounds and the hardships of war'; 'nevertheless he had summoned up all his strength and in the first days ordered everything personally by day and by night, but only to collapse afterwards into all the greater slackness, to which were added grief at the misfortune of the state and vexation at the dissolution of all discipline, all of which had shaken him deeply, who had grown great in the old strict Prussian school'; 'for the rest the governor was a proud, hard man, feared by his subordinates, who at this time, however, had turned his confidence chiefly to General Count Wartensleben, who had stayed behind in the fortress, who seems early on to have wished for a speedy surrender and, according to Marshal Ney's report to Napoleon, is said to have told the French parlementaire, who complained to him of the old governor's obstinacy, as early as 23 October: \"First throw plenty of bombs and shells into the town, and the obstinate governor will surely change his mind.\"'; 'taken from the correspondence of Marshal Ney to Napoleon intercepted at Gutstadt in 1807, from which it also appears that the marshal made every arrangement to see some mortars brought before Magdeburg as quickly as possible'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Klein Ottersleben, 23 October 1806'; 'General Wartensleben, sent by the King of Prussia to this governor, told adjutant-commandant Lefol in confidence that he hoped to succeed in making him listen to reason if a few shells were fired on the place'; 'commandant was Colonel dü Trossel, who stood in complete dependence on the governor and was seldom informed by him of any negotiations and orders'; 'of bread flour there was a stock for 3 months; of grain there could be no lack, given the great stores in this trading town; on the other hand the governor had neglected, in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October, when the complete investment first took place, to supply himself from the rich country on the right bank of the Elbe with sufficient fresh meat and the other provisions, for which the confusion in the fortress until the complete departure of the Hohenlohe troops may at first have been to blame'; 'Ney's corps hardly had the strength of the garrison, and at the moment only 900 men of cavalry at its disposal, but the governor had too little confidence in his men to bring himself to an active defence'; 'I have had Lieutenant General de Kleist, governor of Magdeburg, summoned; his answer was negative'; 'M. de Kleist has moreover given his word not to seek to thwart the operations of the French armies provided the movements take place out of range of his cannon'; 'as early as the 23rd the marshal had summoned the governor to surrender; the governor asked on the 27th for a meeting, which took place on the 28th between him and General Vandamme but had no result'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'on the 31st the garrison made a foraging expedition along the right bank of the Elbe towards the Herrenkrug'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'on the 31st the enemy made a sortie by Friedrichstadt, on the right bank of the Elbe; it was made up of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns. The enemy, after forming up in line between Crakau and Prester, carried off 6 wagons of forage and went back into the place immediately afterwards'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the governor expressed to me the wish to send one of his officers to Berlin to learn the situation of the Prussian army, so as to take a decision either for the defence of the place or for the capitulation. I had agreed to this request on the condition that on this officer's return the town would capitulate. The governor has not spoken of it again'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'the governor renewed to me yesterday the request for a passport for one of his aides-de-camp, whom he wished to send'; 'to Berlin to make sure of the situation of the Prussian armies; he proposed a cessation of arms until this officer's return. I offered this passage on the condition that the town would surrender as soon as it was proved that there was no longer a Prussian army; this condition was not accepted'; Höpfner, as in claim side-a-command for the summons of the 5th; 'the governor answered: he could not enter into anything until he had really convinced himself of the dissolution of the army by sending a Prussian officer; until that officer's return, however, he would conclude an armistice'; 'on 6 November the marshal sent his aide-de-camp Liger-Belair and Captain Regnard to Magdeburg, accompanied by Major Wedell of the Leib-Kürassier regiment, who had been taken prisoner at Prenzlau'; 'the governor at once assembled the generals present in Magdeburg and the commandant, laid before them the correspondence with Marshal Ney, had Major Wedell give an account of the events in the army on the march to the Oder, and announced his decision to capitulate'; 'the way in which the governor handled the whole matter seemed to be nothing more than a communication of his decision; he asked no advice of the generals, curtly rejected all objections, and formally ordered the meeting to sign the protocol drawn up'; 'when General Alvensleben asked what they had actually been called for, and remarked that they still lacked nothing, that they all still had red cheeks etc., the governor silenced him with the words: \"Major General v. Alvensleben, you are the youngest in this circle; speak when you are asked.\"'; 'it was rightly expected that a formal council of war would still be held, to which by regulation all the staff officers of the garrison had to be called'; 'neither the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, nor the artillery officer of the place, Major Hüser, had been called to the conference'; 'the negotiations were continued. The engineer of the place represented to the governor that the fortress could not be taken by a coup de main, that despite its poor profile it could hold out in a regular siege for 4—5'; 'weeks after the opening of the trenches, that the enemy had as yet prepared nothing for a siege, which needed a considerable time, and that he should therefore not hurry anything at all'; 'it was all in vain. The governor answered that he held himself convinced by Major Wedell of the hopelessness of a relief, and must therefore capitulate out of humanity'; 'except General Count Wartensleben, the senior general after the governor, all the generals had shown themselves more or less averse to the surrender of the fortress'; 'on the afternoon of the 7th an armistice was signed on the Prussian side by General Renouard, Colonel dü Trossel and Captain Leblank, and all work in the fortress was stopped'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönebeck, 8 November 1806'; 'done in duplicate at Magdeburg, 7 November 1806'; 'du Troussel, colonel, commandant of the place of Magdeburg'; 'Le Blanc, captain in the regiment of Prince Louis of Prussia'; 'and Messrs. de Renouard, major general, chief of an infantry regiment and knight of the order of Military Merit of Prussia (du Troussel and Leblanc), stipulating in the name of His Excellency Count de Kleist, general of infantry, knight of the orders of the Black Eagle and of the Red Eagle of Prussia and of that of Saint Alexander Nevsky of Russia, and military governor of the town and citadel of Magdeburg'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'on the 5th I made my last summons to the governor, and on the 6th the parleys began. I have today sent a draft capitulation; M. de Kleist has assembled his council of war; it seems that opinions there are divided; but despite the delays this causes, I hope to have a definite answer shortly'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Schönbeck, 8 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'the governor raised difficulties up to the moment of signing; there were two parties in the place, that of the magistrates and the inhabitants, which wished to capitulate, and that of the officers, which insisted on resistance. This diversity'; 'of opinions hampered the negotiation and prolonged the conferences'; '29th Bulletin of the Grande Armée'; 'Berlin, 9 November 1806'; 'Marshal Ney, charged with the siege of Magdeburg, had this place bombarded. Several houses having been burned, the inhabitants showed their discontent, and the commandant asked to capitulate'.",

      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Bodart records the capitulation of Magdeburg on 8 November, after which the whole garrison went into captivity, 16 generals and 800 officers being released on parole. Höpfner: on the afternoon of the 7th an armistice was signed and all work in the fortress stopped; on the 8th General Dütaillis, Ney's chief of staff, came into the fortress in the afternoon, and at 1 o'clock the capitulation was concluded; on the 10th the French occupied the Ulrich gate, and on the 11th the garrison laid down its arms and was marched to Bernburg in 4 equally strong columns, each escorted by 6 companies of infantry and 20 cavalrymen, an infantry regiment following in reserve. The armistice Foucart prints, made between Marshal Ney and Lieutenant General Count de Kleist as being agreed on the main points of the capitulation that was to put the place and citadel in the French army's power, runs from 7 November and was done at Magdeburg that day; on 8 November Ney sent a copy of the armistice concluded 'last night' and wrote that his officers in the place were settling the capitulation on the basis already agreed, that the garrison would be prisoners and sent to France except the officers, who would return home on parole, and that it would defile on the 11th. In a second letter that day he wrote that the fortress surrendered and the capitulation had been signed that evening. Its articles 1 to 4 hand over the town, citadel and fortifications with their artillery, munitions, magazines, supplies and public property; give the Ulrich gate and its outworks to the French on 10 November in the afternoon; have the garrison march out by the Ulrich gate on the morning of 11 November with the honours of war and 4 field pieces and lay down its arms; and make it prisoners of war, the soldiers to be taken to France and the officers prisoners on parole not to serve before exchange, free to go where they chose, those with families who were settled and married in Magdeburg being allowed to stay. Its date line is Magdeburg, 8 November 1806. The 29th Bulletin, of 9 November, says the commandant asked to capitulate after the bombardment; the Emperor wrote that day that Magdeburg had surrendered on the 7th; the 30th Bulletin, of 10 November, that it surrendered on the 8th and its gates were occupied by the French on the 9th. Ney reported on 11 November that the garrison, in 4 columns, began to defile at 9 in the morning and finished at 3 in the afternoon, each column being sent to Bernburg under an escort of 6 companies of infantry under a chef de bataillon and 25 cavalrymen, with General Roguet in overall command; Roguet's memoirs, in Foucart's footnote, give him 18 companies under 3 chefs de bataillon and 2 guns, and say the operation was finished only at 6 in the evening and that he organised 8 columns. The 31st Bulletin: the garrison defiled on the 11th at 9 in the morning before Ney's corps. The Emperor congratulated Ney on 12 November on the happy surrender of Magdeburg.",

      "rationale": "The frozen frame outcome with Höpfner's account and the French documents, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription); no source read gives a different result. The date and the timings differ and are kept as given: the capitulation is dated 8 November by Bodart, Höpfner, Ney's letters, its own date line and the 30th Bulletin, and 'the 7th', the armistice's date, by the Emperor's letter of 9 November; Höpfner's 'at 1 o'clock' after an arrival in the afternoon does not say which 1 o'clock, and Ney says the capitulation was signed in the evening; Höpfner has the armistice signed on the afternoon of the 7th, Ney's letter 'last night'; the gates were to be occupied on the 10th (article 2; Höpfner), but the 30th Bulletin has them occupied on the 9th; and the defile ran from 9 to 3 in 4 columns with 25 cavalrymen each (Ney), in 4 columns with 20 (Höpfner), or until 6 in the evening in 8 columns (Roguet). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and '16 generals and 800 officers were released on parole'; 'capitulation of Magdeburg on 8 November'; 'on the afternoon of the 7th an armistice was signed on the Prussian side by General Renouard, Colonel dü Trossel and Captain Leblank, and all work in the fortress was stopped'; 'on the 8th General Dütaillis, chief of staff of Marshal Ney, came into the fortress in the afternoon, and at 1 o'clock the capitulation was concluded'; 'on the 10th the French occupied the Ulrich gate, and on the 11th the garrison laid down its arms and was set marching to Bernburg in 4 equally strong columns, each under the escort of 6 companies of infantry and 20 cavalrymen; an infantry regiment followed the escort in reserve'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. It shall lay down its arms, and the cavalry shall hand over its arms and its horses at the place to be agreed, within cannon range of the place'; '4. — Once the arms are laid down, the garrison shall be prisoners of war; the soldiers shall be taken to France, and the officers shall be prisoners on their word of honour not to serve, before exchange, against His Majesty the Emperor of the French and King of Italy, nor against his allies, and they shall be free to withdraw to the places they designate.       "value": "Side A's (French) loss in Ney's reports: his daily report of 2 November says the enemy's heavy cannonade on his entrenched posts caused neither killed nor wounded from the 26th to the 28th, nor on the 29th at Vandamme's posts; that on the 30th and 31st, in carrying small posts, his troops had 2 men killed and 3 wounded; and that in the night of 31 October to 1 November Marchand's raid and the general reconnaissance cost neither killed nor wounded. No passage read gives a French loss for the days from 3 November to the capitulation, including the fighting at the Neustadt on 4 November and in the night to the 5th, or a total for side A, and Bodart prints none.",

      "rationale": "Side A's reports, read from the page images. They cover only parts of the investment and are not a total; Colbert's raid of the same night is given no loss. For the night of 4 to 5 November Ney's letter of 7 November reports a Prussian sortie sharply repulsed, and Höpfner French attacks on the Neustadt repulsed and repeated in vain, neither with a French loss (claim posture). English renderings (ours): 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'the 26th, 27th and 28th were spent compelling the enemy's advanced posts on both banks of the Elbe to withdraw immediately under the cannon of the place; from then on the blockade was complete'; 'the enemy cannonaded our posts heavily; but as they are entrenched, there were neither killed nor wounded'; 'on the 29th the same cannonade by the enemy on the posts of General Vandamme, entrenched within musket range of Neustadt: neither killed nor wounded'; 'the 30th and the 31st were spent carrying some small enemy posts; some thirty men were taken, and as many killed or wounded. We had 2 men killed and 3 wounded'; 'in the same night of the 31st to 1 November General Marchand had an enemy post of 15 grenadiers, furnished by that of the Closterberg, carried; the enemy also had 4 killed and 6 wounded. We had neither killed nor wounded'; 'a general reconnaissance combined with General Vandamme's troops took place that same night along the whole length of the blockade line on the left bank of the Elbe and up to the ditches of the place. Its main object was to carry posts, but the enemy had taken the precaution of withdrawing them at the evening gun. The musketry was fairly brisk; we had neither killed nor wounded'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'great exactness reigns in the service, and the result is that the enemy, after attempting several sorties, has not managed to take a single prisoner from us'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806' (his second letter of that date); 'in the night of the 4th to the 5th the 2nd division took up arms.       "id": "side-b-losses",
      "dimension": "outcome",
      "value": "Side B (Prussian) lost the fortress and its garrison. Bodart: the whole garrison went into captivity, 16 generals and 800 officers being released on parole, and besides the 577 guns the French took 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, 54 flags and 5 standards. Höpfner, from Ney's report: 22,000 men of all arms, 20 generals and 800 officers were taken in Magdeburg, with 700 cannon, 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, iron in abundance, a pontoon train, 54 flags and 5 standards and several silver trumpets, and 346 foreign flags and 10 such standards were found in the arsenal; among the guns were 39 position guns of the field artillery. He names the generals present at the governor's conference and the others taken prisoner. Ney, 11 November: each of the 4 columns exceeded 4,000 men, and with 2,000 artillerymen, 400 cuirassiers, 20 generals and about 800 officers the whole could be put without exaggeration at 22,000 men; he held 54 infantry flags and 5 standards, others having been broken; the fortress held 700 guns, a million livres of powder, a very great quantity of cast iron, a train of 90 pontoons and flour. The 30th Bulletin: 16,000 men, nearly 800 guns and magazines of every kind fell into French hands. The 31st Bulletin: 20 generals, 800 officers, 22,000 prisoners, among them 2,000 artillerymen, 54 flags, 5 standards, 800 guns, a million of powder, a great bridge train and an immense matériel of artillery. Roguet's memoirs, in Foucart's footnote, say that 20,000 prisoners reached the Rhine. Before the capitulation, Ney's daily report gives some thirty men taken and as many killed or wounded on the 30th and 31st, and a post of 15 grenadiers carried by Marchand, with 4 more killed and 6 wounded, in the night of 31 October to 1 November.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "post_outcome",
      "rationale": "Separate accounts read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription), not combined. Bodart's powder, bombs, flags and standards are the figures Höpfner gives from Ney's report, but his guns are the 577 of Höpfner's garrison return, not the report's 700 (our comparison); which source Bodart used was not checked. Ney's letter of 11 November and the report Höpfner cites agree on 22,000 men, 20 generals, 800 officers, 700 guns, a million of powder, 54 flags and 5 standards, but the letter read has no bombs, trumpets or arsenal flags, so Höpfner's report may be another document or a fuller copy (not checked). Höpfner names the governor and 15 other generals as present at the conference or taken prisoner, 16 in all, the number of generals Bodart has released on parole (our count and comparison); the 20 generals of Ney and the 31st Bulletin are kept as given. The sentence on the Rhine opens the third paragraph of Foucart's footnote; the paragraph between was not transcribed, and the rest of the third paragraph, seen only in the OCR, goes on in Roguet's first person, so it is read as his. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength, and '16 generals and 800 officers were released on parole'; 'besides the 577 guns the French took 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, 54 flags, 5 standards'; 'according to Marshal Ney's report, 22,000 men of all arms, 20 generals and 800 officers were taken prisoner in Magdeburg, 700 cannon, 1 million pounds of powder, 80,000 filled bombs, iron in abundance, a pontoon train, 54 flags and 5 standards and several silver trumpets were taken, and in the arsenal there were also found 346 foreign flags and 10 such'; 'standards'; 'among the guns taken were 39 position guns of the field artillery'; 'of generals there had been present at the conference besides the governor: Count Wartensleben, Renouard, Tschepe, Alvensleben, Schack and Schimonski as active generals; General Count Kunheim and General Holtzendorf as sick and wounded'; 'in addition the generals Müffling, Kaufberg, Ernest, Wedell, Bünting, Reitzenstein and Count Henckel were taken prisoner, some seriously ill, some wounded'; 'Marshal Ney to the Emperor. Magdeburg, 11 November 1806'; 'the 4 columns were equalised in strength as far as possible; each of them exceeded 4,000 men, so that, including 2,000 artillerymen, 400 cuirassiers, 20 generals and about 800 officers, the whole can be put without exaggeration at 22,000 men. I have in my hands 54 flags of in-'; 'fantry and 5 standards; others were broken; I shall await Your Majesty's orders to send them to you'; 'the fortress contains 700 guns, a million livres of powder, a very great quantity of cast iron, a train of 90 pontoons and flour'; '30th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 10 November 1806'; '16,000 men, nearly 800 guns, magazines of every kind fall into our power'; '31st Bulletin of the Grande Armée.     {
      "id": "magdeburg-ground",
      "dimension": "terrain",
      "value": "Bodart places Magdeburg, a town in Prussia and capital of the province of Saxony, on the Elbe. Höpfner: by the works undertaken since the end of April 1806 the main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had been palisaded, many works of the outer enceinte linked by palisades, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, so that with any serious resistance the fortress could be taken only by a formal attack; only the suburbs could not resist long, and the entrenchments near them were to hold the enemy only until the inhabitants had saved their belongings, after which the suburbs were to be burned, though their many massive ruins would still block the view. Buildings that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and Neustadt were pulled down from the 29th and the rest burned that night. On the right bank the garrison foraged towards the Herrenkrug, Kolbert set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester, and the French posts were pushed to 12—1500 paces from the glacis, with supports at Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau and reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern; on the left bank Marchand commanded the position upstream, with his quarters at Gr. Ottersleben, and Vandamme downstream at Olvenstädt. Ney: the extent of the fortifications was immense; the bridges at Schönebeck and over the old Elbe at Plötzky let his corps cross without being disturbed; Friedrichstadt lay on the right bank, where Colbert surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester and the farms nearer the place; Colbert's posts stood one and a half cannon ranges from the place, and Vandamme's posts were entrenched within musket range of Neustadt; on 7 November Colbert, with his headquarters at Gommern, commanded on the right bank, Marchand was at Gross-Ottersleben and Vandamme had his headquarters at Olvenstadt, his left resting on the Elbe; works of the place protected Sudenburg and the Closterberg; and the musketry and cannonade of almost every night were between Neustadt and Diesdorf.",
      "status": "supported",
      "phase": "inherited",
      "rationale": "Location and works as described, read from the page images. No plan of Magdeburg was inspected (Ney's plan of the blockade, sent on 7 November, was not seen), and where each work stood is taken only from the narratives. Ney gives the distance of the posts in cannon ranges and Höpfner in paces; they are not converted. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, on the Elbe, capital of the province of Saxony)'; 'despite the earlier, highly dilapidated state and the faulty construction of the works, Magdeburg had nevertheless been brought, by the corrective works undertaken since the end of April 1806 and by the activity of the engineer of the place, Captain Kleist, to the point that the whole main fortress and the Stern and Thurm redoubts had received a sound palisading, all the barriers had been hung, the barricades and communication bridges finished, all damaged and missing parapets put in order, many works of the outer enceinte linked together by strong palisadings, their salients bonneted and the ditches closed at their outlet to the Elbe, and in general the fortress was in such a state that, with any serious resistance, it could be taken only by a formal attack'; 'only the suburbs were not in a position to offer a long resistance. But the intention was only to hold up the enemy by the entrenchments built near them until the inhabitants had found time to save their belongings. Then the suburbs were to be burned down, although the many massive ruins would still block the free view'; 'on the 29th they began to have some buildings pulled down that hindered the defence of the Sudenburg and the Neustadt; the rest was burned down in the night. The enemy'; 'on the 31st the garrison made a foraging expedition along the right bank of the Elbe towards the Herrenkrug'; 'General Kolbert, who commanded on the right bank, gathered in the following night 600 men of light infantry, 2 companies of voltigeurs and 2 squadrons, attacked the Prussian outposts at 3 o'clock in the morning of 1 November, drove them back into the fortress and set fire to the villages of Krakau and Prester'; 'the French posts on the right bank were now pushed forward to a distance of 12—1500 paces from the glacis, the supports in Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs and Pechau, reserves at Gerwisch, Woltersdorf, Nedlitz and Gommern'; 'on the left bank General Marchand commanded the position upstream and had his quarters in Gr. Ottersleben, General Vandamme downstream at Olvenstädt'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 3 November 1806'; 'General Vandamme's division is absolutely insufficient to blockade Magdeburg on both banks of the Elbe, the extent of the fortifications being immense. I have gone over all the positions that it is indispensable to occupy: those of the right bank require fewer men, yet there is not a quarter of the troops needed at that point; and in case of a sortie General Colbert would be forced to fall back on Pechau and Gommern while awaiting the help I would send him from the 2nd division'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 25 October 1806'; 'the bridge at Schönebeck is perfectly established, as is the one over the old Elbe at Plötzky; this construction gives me the means of crossing the river with my army corps without the enemy being able in any way to disturb me'; 'daily report on the blockade of Magdeburg. Schönebeck, 2 November 1806'; 'on the 31st the enemy made a sortie by Friedrichstadt, on the right bank of the Elbe; it was made up of about 600 infantry, 50 cuirassiers and 2 guns. The enemy, after forming up in line between Crakau and Prester, carried off 6 wagons of forage and went back into the place immediately afterwards'; 'in the night of the 31st to 1 November General Colbert, with 600 men of the 6th light and 2 voltigeur companies of the 39th, supported by 1 squadron of hussars and chasseurs and 2 four-pounders, approached Friedrichstadt out of cannon range and surrounded the villages of Crakau and Prester, as well as all the farms nearer the place'; 'General Colbert's posts are at one and a half cannon ranges from the place, and the service is done so that nothing can come out of it. His main posts occupy Biederitz, Alt- and Neu-Königsborn, Menz, Gübs, Zippeleben and Pechau'; 'on the 29th the same cannonade by the enemy on the posts of General Vandamme, entrenched within musket range of Neustadt: neither killed nor wounded'; 'if the works of the place that protect Sudenburg and Closterberg prevent us from keeping these 2 points, they will be set on fire, so that the enemy cannot draw any resource from them and is obliged to take in their population, which is already too considerable in Magdeburg for us not to hope for a general revolt if I receive some mortars to bombard the town'; 'Marshal Ney'; 'Marshal Ney to the major general. Schönebeck, 7 November 1806'; 'General Colbert, whose headquarters are at Gommern, commands on the right bank'; 'General Marchand is established at Gross-Ottersleben'; 'General Vandamme has his headquarters at Olvenstadt, resting his left on the Elbe'; 'musketry and cannonade are repeated almost every night between Neustadt and Diesdorf, which tired the garrison of Magdeburg extremely. I have signal rockets fired twice each'.",

      "value": "Side B (Prussian), in Höpfner: the fortress had 577 guns and abundant ammunition but no miners; there was bread flour for 3 months and, in this trading town, no lack of grain, but the governor had neglected to bring in fresh meat and other provisions from the right bank in the 10 days from 18 to 27 October. The bearer of Ney's summons of 23 October reported little siege artillery but 40 to 50 field pieces; the Emperor wrote on 7 November, after ordering Ney to bombard Magdeburg, that all the letters from Stettin asserted that 'the place' was not provisioned and lacked the most important things; the 29th Bulletin put much artillery, considerable magazines and many regimental chests in the fortress, but Ney wrote on 11 November that by his information the regimental chests had followed Prince Hohenlohe's corps on its passage through Magdeburg, and that no trace of the Prince of Hesse's treasure had yet been found. Side A (French): Ney wrote on 25 October that his corps's provisions were assured. He asked for mortars on 30 October, and on 2 November the 4 he had asked of General Clarke arrived with their supply (Höpfner has 4 mortars brought from Erfurt); General Marchand wrote that he had no means to have the ladders shod. The Emperor ordered on 7 November 6 twenty-four-pounders and 2 mortars sent from Wittenberg, noting powder and bombs in quantity at Dresden and 500 milliers of powder at Wittenberg; on 8 November Ney wrote that he had not thought he should countermand that artillery before the capitulation was signed, and would do so then.",
